pages.text: Layla Al-Harbi had never been the type of student who borrowed books nobody else wanted, but on that humid Tuesday afternoon in Jeddah, the library had nothing else left. Every copy of the new chemistry revision guide had already been snapped up by her classmates, who were all on tenterhooks about the mid-term exams. Tucked away on the bottom shelf, wedged between a dusty atlas and a dictionary missing its cover, she found an old edition of Advanced Chemistry with a cracked spine. She almost put it back, assuming it would be hopelessly out of date. Then it fell open in her hands, and she noticed that almost every margin was covered in tiny, slanted handwriting. Curiosity got the better of her, and she checked it out before she could change her mind.

That evening, instead of revising, Layla found herself reading the annotations as though they were chapters of a novel. The writer was meticulous but also surprisingly cheeky, scribbling comments such as 'The textbook overcomplicates this, so try working backwards' and 'Whoever wrote this chapter clearly hated students.' Out of sheer stubbornness, she tested the shortcut on page 112, and to her astonishment, it worked perfectly. On the inside of the back cover, however, she discovered something entirely different. Someone had drawn a careful sketch of a water filter built in layers of sand, gravel, charcoal and date-palm fibre. Beneath it, in the same handwriting, were the words: 'Project unfinished. If you're reading this, please finish it for me. — H., 1999.'

'You're reading far too much into it,' said Noura the next morning, flicking through the pages with a sceptical frown. 'It's probably just some student who got bored during a lesson.' Layla shook her head and pointed out that bored students didn't usually label their diagrams with exact measurements. 'Look at this,' she insisted. 'She's even worked out how much water it could clean per hour, so this wasn't a doodle, it was a plan.' Noura sighed in the way she always did when she knew she was about to be dragged into something. 'Fine,' she conceded, 'but if this ruins my exam results, you're the one explaining it to my mother.'

Their first stop was Mrs. Aisha, the librarian, who had worked at the school for longer than anyone could remember. She peered at the book over her glasses and then disappeared into a storeroom, returning with a battered ledger of old borrowing records. In 1999, the book had been borrowed again and again by the same student, but the ink had faded so badly that only the initial 'H' and the class '3B' were still legible. Mrs. Aisha then pulled out a framed photograph from that year's science fair, which showed a row of girls standing proudly beside their projects. At the end of the row stood an empty table with a handwritten sign that simply read 'Withdrawn.' Layla felt a strange shiver run down her spine, as if the mystery had suddenly become much more real.

With the head teacher's permission, the two girls began staying behind after school to build the filter in the chemistry lab. Their early attempts were nothing short of a disaster, and the water that trickled out of the bottom was even murkier than when they had poured it in. On their fourth try, Noura knocked over a beaker of charcoal powder, and a black cloud settled over everything, including Layla's white headscarf. They were still coughing and laughing when the door swung open. Standing there was Ms. Hessa, the most notoriously demanding teacher in the school, whose red pen was feared by every student in Year Twelve. 'Would either of you care to explain,' she asked coldly, 'why my laboratory looks like the inside of a chimney?'

Layla stammered out an apology and, not knowing what else to do, held up the old textbook with its sketch. Ms. Hessa's expression changed in an instant, though Layla couldn't quite tell whether she was angry or simply stunned. She took the book in both hands and studied the diagram for a long, uncomfortable moment without saying a word. 'Where did you get this?' she finally asked, in a voice that was barely above a whisper. When Layla explained about the library, the teacher closed the book gently and handed it back. 'Your charcoal layer is in the wrong place,' she said quietly, before turning and walking out without another word.

The following afternoon, to the girls' utter disbelief, Ms. Hessa appeared at the lab door with her sleeves rolled up and announced that she would be supervising them from then on. Over the next few weeks, she pushed them relentlessly, insisting that they record every measurement and justify every decision. Yet she was also patient in a way they had never seen in lessons, and occasionally she even cracked a joke. One afternoon, as she wrote a formula on the whiteboard, Layla noticed the unusual way she curled the tail of every letter 'q.' It was exactly the same as the handwriting in the margins of the textbook. Layla glanced at Noura, whose wide eyes told her she had spotted it too.

After Noura had gone home that evening, Layla gathered her courage and asked the question that had been keeping her awake. 'It was you, wasn't it? You're H.' Ms. Hessa was silent for a while, and then she smiled in a way that made her look much younger. She explained that two days before the 1999 science fair, her father had been taken seriously ill, and her family had had to travel to Riyadh so that he could receive treatment. By the time they returned, the fair was over and her momentum was gone, so she wrote that note and slipped the book back onto the shelf. 'I suppose I hoped someone like me would find it one day,' she admitted, 'though I never imagined it would take twenty-five years.'

In March, the three of them carried the finished filter into the regional science competition, where dozens of schools had set up their projects in an enormous exhibition hall. When the judges arrived, Layla poured a jug of cloudy, brown water into the top while Noura explained the science behind each layer. For a few agonising seconds nothing happened at all, and Layla was convinced they were about to be humiliated. Then clear, sparkling water began to drip steadily into the glass below, and one of the judges actually started to applaud. They described the design as both ingenious and affordable, perfect for villages without reliable access to clean water. When their school's name was announced as the winner, Ms. Hessa had to turn away for a moment to compose herself.

A week later, Layla returned the old textbook to the library, but not before adding a few words of her own on the very last page. Underneath Ms. Hessa's note, she wrote: 'Project finished, 2024. Thank you, H. Now it's your turn to start something new. — L.' Mrs. Aisha raised an eyebrow when she saw the book being placed back on the bottom shelf instead of in the archive. 'Some books are meant to keep travelling,' Layla explained, and the librarian nodded as if she understood perfectly. As she walked out into the warm evening air, Layla realised that she had learned far more from those margins than from any revision guide. Somewhere in the future, she hoped, another curious student would pick up that cracked old book and decide to read between the lines.

questions.q: Why did Layla borrow the old chemistry textbook in the first place?
options: All copies of the new revision guide had already been taken.
Ms. Hessa had told her to read it.
She was researching the history of the school.

questions.q: What did the word 'Withdrawn' on the empty table in the 1999 photograph suggest?
options: The project had been disqualified for cheating.
The student had not been able to present her project.
The table was reserved for the judges.

questions.q: In the story, the word 'meticulous' is closest in meaning to:
options: careless and quick
extremely careful and precise
funny and rude

questions.q: What clue finally made Layla realise that Ms. Hessa had written the notes?
options: Ms. Hessa signed her name on the whiteboard.
Mrs. Aisha told her the teacher's old class.
The teacher wrote the letter 'q' in the same unusual way.

questions.q: Why did Layla put the book back on the shelf instead of in the archive?
options: She wanted another student to discover it and be inspired.
Mrs. Aisha refused to keep it in the archive.
She thought the book was no longer useful.

pages.text: Lama Al-Harbi had always believed that the most dangerous thing in her robotics lab was the soldering iron, until the evening her grandfather phoned to thank her for a call she had never made. She was packing away a half-finished sensor when her phone lit up with his name, and she answered expecting his usual gentle teasing about her late hours. Instead, his voice was thick with relief. "Alhamdulillah, you sound like yourself again," he said. "I was beside myself with worry after you rang me crying this afternoon, but don't worry, I've already transferred the money to your friend." Lama stood frozen among the tangled wires, a cold feeling creeping slowly down her spine.

By the time she reached her grandparents' house in north Riyadh, the coffee had gone cold and her grandfather was turning his old prayer beads over and over in his hands. He explained, haltingly, that "Lama" had called from an unknown number, sobbing that she had been in a minor car accident with a classmate's family and needed eight thousand riyals for repairs before the police arrived. "It was your voice, habibti," he insisted, shaking his head in disbelief. "Every word, every little pause, even the way you say 'Jaddi' when you want something." Lama sank onto the cushion beside him, her mind racing. She knew, with sickening certainty, that someone had stolen far more than money; they had stolen her voice.

Only a few months earlier, Lama had written a school report on voice-cloning software, the kind of artificial intelligence that can imitate a person after analysing just a few seconds of their speech. At the time, it had seemed like a fascinating curiosity, something that belonged in films rather than in her grandfather's sitting room. Now she remembered the videos of her debate championship that her school had proudly posted online, hours of her speaking clearly and passionately into a microphone. "They had more than enough material," she murmured, feeling oddly guilty, as though she had left a door wide open. Her father, who had arrived in the meantime, placed a steady hand on her shoulder. "This isn't your fault," he said firmly, "but we'll need your brain to help put it right."

Her father wasted no time, calling the bank's fraud line and then reporting the crime to the authorities, who took down every detail with reassuring seriousness. Meanwhile, her grandfather sat in silence, his pride clearly wounded, and Lama could hardly bear to see a man who had once navigated the desert by the stars looking so lost. "I should have known," he said quietly. "A man of my age, fooled by a machine." Lama took his weathered hand in both of hers. "Jaddi, these programmes fool experts and journalists every day," she told him. "The people who did this are the ones who should feel ashamed, not you."

It turned out that her grandfather, who had a lifelong habit of recording important calls so that he would not forget them, had saved the entire conversation. That weekend, Lama and her cousin Noura, a gifted programmer who could debug code faster than most people could read it, spread out their laptops on the dining table. They converted the recording into a spectrogram, a colourful map of sound frequencies, and compared it with a genuine voice message Lama had sent the week before. At first glance the two were almost identical, but gradually the differences began to emerge. "Look here," Noura said, pointing at the screen. "Real people breathe between sentences, but this voice never takes a single breath, not even while it's supposedly crying."

Before they could celebrate their discovery, Lama's mother received a call that made everyone in the house hold their breath. It was "Lama" again, claiming that the repairs had cost more than expected and begging for another five thousand riyals as quickly as possible. Her mother, thinking on her feet, kept the caller talking while Lama, sitting just metres away, grabbed a notepad and scribbled a question. The officer handling their case had advised them that, if the scammers called back, they should stay calm and gather as much information as they could. Her mother glanced at the note, nodded almost imperceptibly, and switched the phone to speaker.

"Before I send anything, sweetheart," her mother said in a voice of remarkable calm, "tell me the name of the falcon your grandfather kept when you were little." There was a pause on the line, slightly too long, followed by a tearful sound that seemed almost convincing. "Mama, please, there's no time for games!" the voice pleaded. Lama, however, knew that the real answer was Sahab, a name she had chosen herself at the age of six, and one that appeared nowhere online. Her mother repeated the question twice more, and each time the voice dodged it, until at last the line went dead. In that silence, the whole family exchanged a look of grim triumph: the machine could copy Lama's voice, but it could not borrow her memories.

Crucially, during the call the scammers had sent new bank details by text message, which Lama's father immediately forwarded to the bank and the investigators. Together with the spectrogram analysis that Lama and Noura had carefully documented, this evidence helped the authorities link the case to several similar frauds across the region. Weeks went by with little news, and Lama found herself checking her phone constantly, half dreading and half hoping for an update. Then, one evening, her father came home with an expression she had not seen in a long time. "They've traced the account," he announced, "and most of your grandfather's money is being returned." Her grandfather laughed for the first time in weeks, a deep, warm sound that filled the entire house.

When her principal heard what had happened, she invited Lama to give a presentation to students and their families at the end of term. Standing on the same stage where her debate videos had been filmed, Lama felt a flicker of irony, but she spoke with quiet confidence. She explained how voice cloning worked, why hearing a familiar voice was no longer proof of identity, and how every family should agree on a secret question or code word. "Technology itself isn't the villain," she told the audience. "The same tools that tricked my grandfather helped us catch the people who did it." In the front row, her grandfather sat with his chin raised high, applauding louder than anyone else in the hall.

That night, the family gathered on her grandparents' rooftop beneath a sky scattered with stars, sharing dates and cardamom coffee as a cool breeze drifted across the city. Her grandfather produced his old phone and, with a mischievous smile, asked Lama to record a short message in her own voice, one he could keep alongside his recordings of the call. "So that I always remember the difference," he explained. Lama thought for a moment, then spoke softly into the microphone about Sahab, the falcon, and the morning they had watched it soar above the dunes together. When she finished, her grandfather's eyes were shining. "No machine on earth could have said that," he whispered, and Lama knew he was absolutely right.

questions.q: How did the scammers most likely get enough samples to copy Lama's voice?
options: From videos of her debate championship posted online
From secretly recording her in the robotics lab
From her grandfather's recorded phone calls

questions.q: What important clue did Lama and Noura find in the spectrogram?
options: The fake voice spoke much faster than Lama
The fake voice never took a breath between sentences
The fake voice used words Lama never says

questions.q: In the story, what does the phrase "thinking on her feet" suggest about Lama's mother?
options: She was too nervous to sit down
She reacted quickly and cleverly without preparation
She walked around the room while talking

questions.q: Why was the question about the falcon an effective test?
options: The answer was a personal memory that could not be found online
Falcons are difficult for AI programmes to pronounce
The scammers did not speak Arabic

questions.q: What can we infer from the grandfather's request at the end of the story?
options: He wants to use the recording to report the scammers again
He no longer trusts any technology at all
He has regained his confidence and values the genuine connection with Lama

stories.title: The Flood That Came from a Clear Sky

pages.text: On the flat roof of a house in a small village in the Asir mountains, seventeen-year-old Faris had built something his classmates found endlessly amusing. It was a home-made weather station: a spinning anemometer, a rain gauge made from a plastic bottle, and a battered barometer he had rescued from a second-hand shop in Abha. Every evening he recorded the readings in a notebook, and every evening his younger sister Lama asked him, with exaggerated seriousness, whether the sky had sent any important messages. His grandfather, Abu Saleh, called the station 'the machine that argues with the sky'. The old man had spent sixty years herding goats and farming terraces on these slopes, and he believed that anyone who needed a machine to understand the weather simply had not been paying attention. Faris, who loved his grandfather dearly, had long ago stopped trying to win that particular debate.

That Friday, the whole extended family had planned a picnic in Wadi Sahban, a wide, sandy valley about half an hour's drive away, where acacia trees offered shade and the children could run freely. The morning was flawless: not a single cloud marked the deep blue sky, and the air smelled of warm stone and dust. Yet when Faris checked his barometer before breakfast, he frowned. The pressure had dropped noticeably overnight, far more sharply than he would have expected on such a calm day. He opened a radar app on his phone and zoomed in on the high peaks to the north-west, where a dense cluster of storm cells had begun to form. 'It's forty kilometres away,' Lama pointed out, peering over his shoulder. 'Unless clouds have learned to read maps, I think we'll survive.'

By late morning, the wadi was full of life and noise. Uncle Mansour had claimed the flattest stretch of sand, right in the middle of the dry riverbed, and was busy lighting charcoal for the grill while the younger cousins chased each other between the trees. Faris tried to join in, but a sense of unease kept tugging at him, and he found himself glancing repeatedly towards the distant mountains. From here, they looked innocent, their summits only slightly blurred by a faint grey haze. 'You've checked that app about twenty times in ten minutes,' Lama remarked, handing him a cup of tea. 'Either you're expecting a storm, or you've got a secret admirer in the meteorology department.' He managed a smile, but the knot in his stomach refused to loosen.

Eventually, Faris decided he could no longer keep his worries to himself, and he approached his uncle. 'Uncle Mansour, I think we should move the picnic up onto the higher ground, just in case,' he said, trying to sound calm rather than alarmist. His uncle looked up at the spotless sky and laughed good-naturedly. 'Just in case of what, Professor? There hasn't been a drop of rain here all week.' Faris explained that it did not need to rain in the wadi at all: if a heavy storm broke over the mountains, the water would pour down countless slopes and channels, all of which funnelled into this very valley. 'The rain falls up there, but the flood arrives down here,' he insisted. Uncle Mansour patted him on the shoulder, told him he worried too much for someone his age, and turned back to the grill.

It was Abu Saleh who noticed the change first, although he had said nothing to anyone. The breeze, which had been drifting lazily up the valley all morning, suddenly reversed direction and turned cool against his face, carrying a faint, earthy smell that he had not encountered in years. A pair of birds that had been nesting in the acacia above them took flight and headed swiftly towards the ridge. Then, so quietly that only someone listening for it would have heard, came a low murmur from somewhere far up the valley, like distant traffic on a motorway that did not exist. The old man rose stiffly to his feet and leaned on his stick. 'In nineteen eighty-two,' he said slowly, 'I watched this wadi swallow a lorry whole on a day exactly like this one.'

Everyone fell silent, for when Abu Saleh spoke in that tone, people listened. 'The boy's machine and my old knees are telling me the same thing,' he declared. 'Pack up everything and get to the high ground. Now.' Uncle Mansour opened his mouth to object, then evidently thought better of it, and within moments the family was hurriedly folding blankets and carrying children up the rocky slope. Faris, however, had spotted another family further down the valley, their four-wheel drive parked directly on the sandy bed. He and Lama sprinted towards them, shouting and waving their arms. The father, a broad man in a white thobe, seemed reluctant at first, clearly suspecting that two teenagers were exaggerating, but something in Faris's face must have convinced him, because he quickly gathered his wife and children and followed them up the bank.

They reached the rocks with barely a minute to spare. At first, the arrival of the water seemed almost harmless: a thin, muddy trickle the colour of strong tea, snaking silently across the sand where the children had been playing. Then the murmur swelled into a deafening roar, and a wall of brown water, perhaps a metre high, came charging around the bend in the valley. It carried branches, rocks and entire uprooted bushes, tossing them about as though they weighed nothing at all. The other family's car, abandoned on the riverbed, was lifted gently off its wheels, spun round once, and dragged downstream until it disappeared from view. Lama gripped her brother's arm so tightly that he would find bruises there the following morning. Above them, astonishingly, the sun was still shining.

For almost an hour, the two families stood together on the rocks, watching the torrent rage through the place where, only moments before, they had been laughing and grilling meat. The flat stretch of sand Uncle Mansour had chosen was now buried beneath fast-flowing water, and his portable grill had long since vanished. The father of the other family, whose name turned out to be Abu Khalid, came over and shook Faris's hand firmly. 'A car can be replaced,' he said, his voice not entirely steady, 'but my children cannot. May Allah reward you.' Faris, unsure how to respond, simply nodded, overwhelmed by the realisation of how narrowly disaster had been avoided. Beside him, Lama had quietly begun filming the flood, her usual sarcasm replaced by a thoughtful silence.

By the time the water had subsided to a sluggish, muddy stream, the Civil Defence had arrived to check that nobody had been caught in the flood. One of the officers listened to the story with great interest and remarked that, in his experience, most people who died in flash floods never saw a single raindrop before the water reached them. That evening, Lama's video was shared thousands of times, and a local news channel even contacted the family asking for an interview. Uncle Mansour, who had been unusually quiet all afternoon, finally cleared his throat over dinner. 'I suppose I owe you an apology, Professor,' he admitted with a sheepish grin. 'From now on, I'll check with you before I so much as light a match.' The whole table burst out laughing, and Faris felt the last of the day's tension finally drain away.

Later that night, Faris climbed onto the roof to record the day's readings, and was surprised to hear slow footsteps on the stairs behind him. Abu Saleh emerged, breathing heavily, and lowered himself onto an old plastic chair beside the weather station. For a long while, he studied the barometer, the rain gauge and the little spinning cups of the anemometer as if seeing them for the first time. 'Teach me to read your machine,' he said at last, 'and I will teach you what the wind smells like before the water comes.' Faris grinned, opened his notebook to a fresh page, and wrote the date at the top. Above them, the stars glittered over the silent mountains, and for once, the sky and the machine seemed to be in complete agreement.

questions.q: What first made Faris suspect that something was wrong with the weather?
options: His barometer showed a sharp drop in pressure
He saw dark clouds directly above the wadi
His grandfather told him a storm was coming

questions.q: Why was the wadi dangerous even though it was not raining there?
options: The sand became unstable in hot weather
Rain falling on the mountains could flow down into the valley
Strong winds could blow the cars over

questions.q: In the story, the word 'subsided' is closest in meaning to:
options: grew stronger
became less intense
changed direction

questions.q: Why did the family finally agree to move to higher ground?
options: The Civil Defence ordered them to leave
Uncle Mansour saw the water coming
Abu Saleh, whom everyone respected, supported Faris's warning

questions.q: What does the ending suggest about Faris and his grandfather?
options: They realise that science and traditional knowledge can complement each other
Faris decides to give up his weather station
Abu Saleh still believes machines are useless

stories.title: The Blue That Came Too Late

pages.text: Noura had always believed that the most interesting things in Riyadh happened after dark, when the heat finally loosened its grip on the city and the conservation lab on the third floor fell almost silent. She had spent the summer volunteering there under her aunt, Dr. Huda, who restored old manuscripts with the patience of someone defusing a bomb. Most of Noura's work was unglamorous: cataloguing fragments, logging humidity readings, and learning never, under any circumstances, to touch a page without gloves. Yet she did not mind, because every evening she was allowed to sit beside her aunt and watch centuries-old paper being coaxed back to life. At home, long after her family had gone to sleep, she practised geometric illumination of her own, filling sketchbooks with interlocking stars and tracing the delicate borders she had admired in the archive. She had never shown these drawings to anyone, convinced they were nothing more than clumsy imitations.

On a Tuesday in late August, a sealed crate arrived from a private collector who wished to sell an astronomical treatise, supposedly copied in the early seventeenth century. Its pages described the movements of the planets, and its margins were decorated with gold leaf and an extraordinary deep blue that seemed almost to glow. "If it's genuine, it will be the centrepiece of the autumn exhibition," Dr. Huda said, lifting the cover with infinite care. The collector's agent, a polished man named Mr. Khalil, had already made it clear that several foreign museums were eager to buy it. He wanted the lab's official verification by the following Sunday, and he did not seem the kind of person who tolerated delays. Noura caught her aunt's slight frown and understood that a week was hardly enough time to examine a manuscript of this importance.

Over the next few days, Noura's task was to photograph every page under different kinds of light, a job that required more concentration than she had anticipated. It was on the fourth evening, while she was magnifying a corner of folio thirty-two, that something struck her as odd. The blue on that page was slightly greener than on the others, and it lay on the paper in a smoother, more even film, as though it had been applied by a different hand. She told herself she was imagining things, since she was a sixteen-year-old volunteer, not an expert, and her aunt had decades of experience. Still, the detail nagged at her all the way home and refused to let her sleep. At two in the morning, she gave up, opened her laptop, and began reading everything she could find about historical pigments.

What she discovered made her sit bolt upright. The brilliant blue used by most illuminators of that period was made from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone ground into powder, and it was so expensive that it was sometimes worth more than gold. However, in the early eighteenth century, a chemist in Berlin had accidentally produced a cheaper synthetic pigment known as Prussian blue, which had a distinctly greenish tone. If folio thirty-two contained Prussian blue, then at least that page could not possibly have been painted in the early sixteen-hundreds. Noura's heart was pounding, because she realised the implications could be enormous, both for the manuscript and for the lab's reputation. Then a far less comfortable thought occurred to her: what if she was wrong and embarrassed her aunt in front of everyone?

The next morning, she hovered by the kettle for so long that Dr. Huda eventually asked whether she intended to make tea or simply stare at it. "I might have noticed something," Noura said, her voice smaller than she would have liked, "but it's probably nothing." Her aunt put down her cup and gave her the kind of look that left no room for excuses. Haltingly at first, then with growing confidence, Noura explained the colour, the texture, and the date of the Berlin discovery. When she had finished, Dr. Huda was quiet for an unbearably long moment. "In this profession," she said at last, "'probably nothing' is the most dangerous phrase there is, so let's find out."

They spent the afternoon running a non-invasive test that analysed the chemical signature of the pigment without damaging a single fibre of the paper. Noura watched the graph appear on the screen, hardly daring to breathe. The result was unmistakable: folio thirty-two contained iron, the tell-tale component of Prussian blue, while every other page showed the mineral profile of genuine lapis lazuli. "Well spotted," her aunt murmured, and those two words meant more to Noura than any trophy she had ever won. Yet Dr. Huda did not look triumphant; she looked troubled. "This tells us one page is later," she explained, "but it doesn't tell us why, and until we know why, we haven't really learned anything."

Mr. Khalil arrived on Thursday, two days early, and his reaction to the news was anything but calm. "A single page out of eighty?" he scoffed, tapping the table impatiently. "You're prepared to jeopardise a sale worth millions because a schoolgirl thinks one colour looks a little green?" Noura felt her cheeks burn, and for a moment she wished the floor would swallow her whole. Dr. Huda, however, did not raise her voice. "The schoolgirl is right, and the science backs her up," she replied evenly. "We will not sign anything until we understand what happened to this book, and if that costs you a buyer, I'm afraid that's a price you'll have to pay."

That evening, Noura examined folio thirty-two once more, this time under ultraviolet light, which can sometimes reveal writing that has faded beyond the reach of the naked eye. Near the inner margin, almost swallowed by the binding, a few faint lines of script slowly emerged, glowing a ghostly violet. Her aunt leaned in, translated them aloud, and then laughed softly in astonishment. The note had been written in 1847 by a bookbinder from Cairo named Yusuf. It explained that this page had been badly damaged by water, and that he had repainted its border as faithfully as he could, adding his name so that no future reader would mistake his work for the original. "He wasn't a forger at all," Noura whispered. "He was being honest with people who hadn't even been born yet."

The discovery transformed the manuscript's story rather than destroying it. Experts confirmed that the rest of the treatise was authentic, and the hidden note turned an ordinary repair into a rare record of how craftsmen in the nineteenth century had cared for the books they inherited. Even Mr. Khalil had the grace to admit, somewhat stiffly, that the item was now more fascinating than before. The lab decided to display the book open at folio thirty-two, with an ultraviolet lamp that visitors could switch on to read Yusuf's message for themselves. Beneath the display case, a small card credited the research team, and Noura was astonished to find her own name printed among them. Her father, who had never quite understood why she spent her summer among dusty papers, read the card three times before saying anything.

On the final night of the summer, Noura finally gathered the courage to show her sketchbooks to her aunt, bracing herself for polite but empty praise. Instead, Dr. Huda turned the pages slowly, pointing out where a line wavered and where a star pattern was genuinely beautiful. "You have the eye and you're developing the hand," she said, "and the rest is simply time." Back at home, Noura completed a new border of interlocking stars, using a blue she had mixed herself. Then, remembering a bookbinder who had lived almost two centuries before her, she wrote her name and the date in tiny script along the inner edge. It was barely visible, but it was there, and it was true. Someday, she thought, someone might find it and know exactly whose hand had made it.

questions.q: What first made Noura suspect that folio thirty-two was different?
options: Its blue was greener and lay in a smoother film than on other pages
Its gold leaf was missing from the margins
Its text described different planets from the rest of the book

questions.q: Why was Prussian blue an important clue?
options: It was more expensive than lapis lazuli
It was only used by bookbinders in Cairo
It was not invented until the early eighteenth century

questions.q: In the story, what does the word 'jeopardise' most nearly mean?
options: To celebrate
To put at risk
To examine carefully

questions.q: What did the hidden note reveal about the repainted page?
options: A forger had tried to raise the book's price
A bookbinder named Yusuf had honestly repaired water damage and signed his work
Mr. Khalil had secretly changed the page before the sale

questions.q: Why does Noura write her name along the inner edge of her own border at the end?
options: She wants to sell her drawing to a museum
Her aunt ordered her to label all her sketches
She has been inspired by Yusuf's honesty and wants her work to be truthfully identified

stories.title: The Night the Beach Went Dark

pages.text: Huda had always assumed that the sea near Umluj kept its secrets to itself, but on the first night of the nesting season it seemed determined to share them with her. She was walking along the shore with her uncle Khalid, a marine biologist who had been monitoring green turtles on this stretch of the Red Sea coast for almost twenty years. Every few metres he paused, shone a dim red torch at the sand, and muttered numbers into a battered notebook. 'Why red?' Huda asked, struggling to keep up as her shoes filled with sand. 'Because turtles barely notice it,' he replied without looking up. 'White light is another matter entirely, and that, my dear niece, is what keeps me awake at night.'

At first Huda found the work painstaking rather than thrilling, since it involved little more than measuring the wide, tractor-like tracks the mother turtles left as they hauled themselves out of the water. Yet when her uncle crouched beside a freshly dug nest and explained that roughly a hundred eggs lay buried beneath their feet, she felt something shift inside her. These creatures, he told her, had been returning to the very beaches where they themselves had hatched for longer than anyone could possibly remember. 'In about two months, the babies will break out and race for the sea,' he said. 'They find it by following the brightest horizon, which, for millions of years, has been moonlight reflected on the water.' Huda glanced over her shoulder at the town glowing faintly behind the dunes, and a small, uneasy question began to take shape in her mind.

That question became considerably harder to ignore in August, when a new seafront café opened just beyond the northern end of the beach. It was a striking building, all glass and pale stone, and its owner had installed a row of powerful floodlights so that families could see the waves breaking long after sunset. Everyone in town seemed delighted, and Huda's younger brother Yousef declared that their mango juice was the best he had ever tasted. What made the situation awkward was that the café belonged to Abu Saleh, an old friend of her father's and the generous man who had sponsored her school's science trip the previous spring. 'Those lights are going to cause trouble,' Uncle Khalid said quietly as they drove past one evening. Huda said nothing, but she noticed that he was gripping the steering wheel rather more tightly than usual.

The trouble arrived sooner than anyone had predicted, on a warm night when Huda and Yousef had joined their uncle for what was supposed to be a routine check. Instead of finding tiny tracks leading neatly down to the water, they found dozens of them curving the wrong way, up the beach, across the dunes and towards the gleaming café. Yousef was the first to spot them: a trail of hatchlings no bigger than his palm, struggling across the tarmac of the coastal road as a car approached in the distance. 'Grab the bucket!' Uncle Khalid shouted, and for the next twenty minutes the three of them scrambled about on their knees, scooping up exhausted babies and checking under bushes with their red torches. By the time they had carried their small, wriggling cargo back to the shoreline, Huda's hands were trembling. She watched the hatchlings vanish into the dark surf and realised she was far too angry to cry.

The following morning, Huda did what she always did when a problem felt overwhelming: she turned it into a project. Over the next fortnight she recorded every nest that hatched, marking on a map which direction the babies had travelled and how many had been found alive. With her uncle's permission, she set up a cheap light meter at several points along the beach and logged the readings each evening. The pattern that emerged was impossible to argue with, as nests closest to the café showed a disorientation rate of almost seventy per cent, while those at the darker southern end showed barely any. 'You've done in two weeks what I've been meaning to do for two years,' her uncle admitted, scrolling through her spreadsheet with obvious pride. 'The question now is what you intend to do with it.'

Huda spent that evening debating the matter with her parents, and the conversation turned out to be more complicated than she had anticipated. Her father was reluctant to embarrass a man who had always treated their family with kindness, and he worried that a public complaint might be seen as ungrateful. 'Abu Saleh isn't a villain,' he pointed out gently. 'He simply doesn't know what you know.' Her mother, on the other hand, reminded them that keeping silent would not make the problem disappear, and that honesty delivered with respect was hardly the same thing as an insult. Eventually they agreed on a compromise: before going anywhere near the municipal council, Huda would speak to Abu Saleh directly, with her father beside her. She lay awake until well after midnight, rehearsing what she would say and dreading every possible reply.

Abu Saleh greeted them warmly, insisted on bringing out tea and dates, and listened without interrupting while Huda explained her findings with the help of her laptop. When she showed him the photograph Yousef had taken of the hatchlings on the road, his smile faded completely. 'I had no idea,' he said slowly, rubbing his beard. 'I thought I was making the beach safer for families, and instead I've been leading these little ones to their deaths.' For a moment Huda feared he might become defensive, but he simply leaned forward and asked, 'So tell me, what would you do in my place?' She had prepared for an argument, not a question, and it took her a second to gather her thoughts. Then she explained that he did not need to plunge his café into darkness; he only needed the right kind of light, pointed in the right direction.

Within a week, workers had replaced the dazzling white floodlights with low, shielded amber lamps that lit the café's terrace without spilling onto the sand. Abu Saleh also planted a hedge of native shrubs along the edge of the dunes, which, as Uncle Khalid explained, would act as a natural screen against the glow of passing cars. Not everyone was convinced, and a few customers grumbled that they could no longer see the waves at night. Abu Saleh, however, had come up with an idea that would turn their complaints on their head. He printed a small sign for every table, illustrated by Yousef, which read: 'We have dimmed our lights so that the turtles can find the sea. Look up instead.' Huda laughed when she saw it, but she also noticed several families quietly tilting their heads towards the sky.

News travels fast in a small town, and before long the municipal council invited Huda to present her research at one of its public meetings. Standing in front of a room full of officials, she felt her voice wobble at first, yet as soon as she began describing that night on the road, her nerves seemed to melt away. She was careful to praise Abu Saleh rather than blame him, explaining that his willingness to change had proved how easily the problem could be solved. Afterwards, the council agreed to introduce turtle-friendly lighting regulations for every new building along the coast, and to hold an annual 'Dark Hour' at the peak of the hatching season. As people filed out of the hall, an elderly fisherman stopped to shake her father's hand. 'Your daughter has given the sea back its moon,' he said, and Huda had to look away to hide how much those words meant to her.

On the night of the first Dark Hour, almost half the town gathered quietly at the top of the beach, the café's amber lamps glowing softly behind them like embers. Huda knelt beside the nest she had been watching for weeks, her uncle on one side and Yousef, barely able to contain his excitement, on the other. At first nothing happened, and then the sand began to tremble and collapse as though something beneath it were breathing. One by one, the hatchlings burst out and paused, as if listening, before turning as a single body towards the silver line where the moonlight touched the water. Nobody spoke; the only sound was the sea, patient and ancient, welcoming them home. Watching the last tiny shape disappear into the waves, Huda understood that protecting the world rarely demanded heroes, only people willing to notice, ask the right questions and, sometimes, simply turn off the lights.

pages.text: Faisal had imagined many ways of spending his sixteenth summer, but standing behind the dusty counter of his grandfather's grocery shop in the old quarter of Taif was not one of them. Grandfather Saleh had broken his hip in a fall during Ramadan, and the doctors had been unusually firm: no lifting, no climbing ladders, and certainly no twelve-hour days behind the till. Someone had to keep the shop open, and since Faisal's older brother was abroad on a scholarship, the task had landed squarely on his shoulders. The shop smelled of cardamom, saffron and old cardboard, and its shelves leaned slightly, as though they were tired of holding up forty years of tinned tomatoes. On his first morning, Faisal sold exactly three bottles of water and a packet of biscuits. By noon, he was convinced that the summer would be the longest of his life.

It did not take a business genius to see why trade was so slow. A gleaming supermarket had opened beside the highway the previous year, with air-conditioned aisles, a car park and prices that his grandfather could never hope to match. Then, on the fourth day, Faisal found an envelope tucked beneath the cash box, addressed in his grandfather's shaky handwriting to the landlord. Inside was an unsent letter, politely asking for yet another month's extension on the rent. Faisal felt his stomach tighten, because he realised that the shop was not merely struggling; it was deep in the red. While rummaging through a drawer for a pen, he came across a thick notebook bound in faded green leather. Its pages were crowded with names, dates and sums of money, written in the meticulous script of a man who had never once missed a day's work.

At first, Faisal assumed the notebook was an ordinary ledger of sales, but he soon understood that it was something quite different. Every entry recorded a debt: a family who had bought rice and cooking oil on credit, a student who had needed school supplies, a widow who had run short before the end of the month. Some lines were written in ordinary blue ink, but a great many had been crossed out with a single, neat stroke of green and marked with one word: settled. Curious, Faisal checked them against the shop's receipts, yet he could find no record of any of those debts ever being paid. He took out his phone and added up the outstanding amounts, and the total made him whistle under his breath. If even half of that money came back, the rent could be paid several times over. With the brisk confidence of someone who has just solved a problem, he decided that he would start collecting the very next day.

The first name on his list was Umm Hamad, who lived two streets away in a narrow house with a blue metal door. When Faisal knocked, it was her son Hamad, a thin boy of about twelve, who opened it and greeted him politely. Through the doorway, Faisal glimpsed a small, spotless room with almost no furniture, and he noticed that the boy's school shoes had been carefully mended with tape. The speech he had rehearsed all morning suddenly dissolved in his mouth. Instead of mentioning money, he heard himself mumbling that he had simply come to say the shop was still open. His second visit, to Ustadh Idris, a retired teacher, went even worse: the old man's face flushed with shame the moment Faisal said his grandfather's name, and Faisal left before he could bring himself to explain why he had come.

That evening, Faisal sat beside his grandfather's bed and, with some embarrassment, confessed what he had been trying to do. To his surprise, the old man did not seem angry; he merely smiled and asked him to bring the green ledger. "A debt written in blue is a promise to remember," he said, tapping the page gently. "A debt crossed out in green is a promise to forget." He explained that he had never told those families their debts were forgiven, because a man who is given charity openly may lose his dignity, but a man who believes he still owes can hold his head high. "So they think they still owe you money?" Faisal asked, incredulous. "They think they owe me something," his grandfather replied, "and perhaps, one day, they will repay it to someone else."

Faisal could not let the matter rest so easily. "But Grandfather, if the shop closes, there will be no one left to be kind to anybody," he argued, his frustration getting the better of him. The old man only sighed and said that the shop had never really been the point. Unable to sleep that night, Faisal took the ledger to the roof and turned its pages slowly under the light of his phone. On the very first page, the handwriting was different: older, rounder and badly faded by time. There, beneath a date from more than forty years earlier, he read a single line: "Saleh, a young man newly arrived from the village, forty riyals." It had been crossed out, unmistakably, in green ink.

The discovery changed something in Faisal, though he could not quite have put it into words. He stopped thinking about the ledger as a list of people who owed his family, and started thinking of it as a long, invisible chain that his grandfather had simply been the latest to carry. Since he could not collect the debts, he resolved to save the shop the hard way. He scrubbed the floors, rearranged the shelves so that the most useful items were within easy reach, and began offering free delivery to elderly neighbours who could no longer walk to the highway. Hamad, who had started dropping by after school, insisted on helping, and Faisal paid him in sandwiches and maths tutoring. It was Hamad, quite innocently, who mentioned to half the neighbourhood that the old shop might have to close by the end of the month.

The following Friday, as the worshippers streamed out of the mosque after the noon prayer, something remarkable began to happen. Ustadh Idris arrived first, his face composed, and pressed a sealed envelope into Faisal's hand, saying only that it was long overdue. Then came a carpenter who, without being asked, spent the afternoon repairing the sagging shelves, and a woman who sent her son with trays of homemade date pastries to be sold at the counter. Last of all, a well-dressed man in his thirties walked in and introduced himself as a former customer who now owned a pharmacy in Riyadh. "When I was a student, your grandfather let me buy my books on credit for an entire year," he said quietly. "I have carried that debt for fifteen years, and today I would like to set it down."

By the end of the month, the rent had been paid in full, and the shop had more customers than it had seen in years, many of them coming not out of pity but because they genuinely preferred its warmth to the cold efficiency of the supermarket. When Grandfather Saleh was finally allowed to leave the house, he walked the short distance to the shop with the help of a cane and Faisal's steady arm. He paused in the doorway and took in the repaired shelves, the queue at the till and Hamad proudly stacking tins in perfectly straight rows. For a long moment he said nothing at all. Then Faisal noticed that his grandfather's eyes had filled with tears, which he did not bother to wipe away. "You see," the old man murmured at last, "nothing given with a good heart is ever truly lost."

A few weeks later, on the last evening before Faisal returned to Riyadh for the new school year, Umm Hamad sent her son to buy flour, sugar and a bag of rice. Hamad counted his coins twice, his cheeks reddening, and admitted that he was several riyals short. Faisal took the green ledger from beneath the counter and wrote the boy's mother's name in careful blue ink, exactly as his grandfather had taught him. Then, when Hamad had gone, he reached for a second pen, the green one, and drew a single neat line through the entry. He wrote the word "settled" beside it and closed the book gently, aware that he had just added his own small link to a chain that had begun long before he was born. Outside, the call to the evening prayer drifted across the rooftops of Taif, and for the first time that summer, Faisal felt entirely at home.

pages.text: Layla had expected the winter holidays to be a quiet affair, but the moment her uncle's dusty four-by-four rattled past the towering sandstone cliffs of AlUla, she sensed that something was stirring. Uncle Khalid, a ranger with the local conservation team, had invited her to spend two weeks at his field station, partly because she had pestered him for months and partly, she suspected, because he needed an extra pair of sharp eyes. The rocks glowed orange in the late afternoon light, carved by wind and time into shapes that looked almost alive. "Keep your eyes open," he said, glancing at her with a half-smile. "Out here, the land tells you its secrets only if you are patient enough to listen." Layla pressed her forehead against the window, determined not to miss a single one.

That evening, over sweet tea and dates, Uncle Khalid spread a map across the table and pointed to a cluster of red dots scattered along the canyons. Each dot marked a camera trap, a motion-activated device strapped to a rock or a bush, designed to photograph whatever wandered past in the dark. "We are looking for the Arabian leopard," he explained, lowering his voice as though the animal itself might overhear. "Their numbers have dwindled so drastically that many experts fear there may be fewer than two hundred left in the entire peninsula." Layla had read about the leopard, an animal so elusive that local people called it the ghost of the mountains. "Has anyone actually seen one here?" she asked. Her uncle hesitated, then admitted that a shepherd had reported strange tracks only a month earlier.

The next morning, they drove to the nearby village to visit Layla's grandfather, Abu Saad, who greeted her with a warm embrace and a lecture about how thin she had become. Yet when Uncle Khalid mentioned the leopard, the old man's face hardened like clay left in the sun. "When I was your age, Layla, a leopard came down from those hills and took four of my father's goats in a single night," he said, tapping his cane against the floor. "Those goats were our livelihood, and that winter we went hungry because of a thief with spots." Layla realised that her grandfather had nursed this grudge for more than sixty years. She wanted to argue that the leopard had only been trying to survive, but the pain in his eyes made her hold her tongue. Instead, she poured him another cup of coffee and quietly resolved to change his mind.

For several days, Layla accompanied her uncle as he checked the cameras, scrambling over boulders and squeezing through narrow gorges where the air was cool even at midday. Most of the photographs showed nothing more exciting than foxes, hares and an occasional curious ibex peering straight into the lens. On the fifth day, however, Layla spotted a large, rounded print pressed into a patch of soft sand beneath an overhanging rock. Nearby, the bark of an acacia tree bore deep scratch marks, as if something powerful had sharpened its claws there. "Don't jump to conclusions," Uncle Khalid warned, though she could tell from the way he crouched over the print that his heart was racing too. He photographed it from every angle and murmured that, if it was what they hoped, it would be the find of his career.

Their excitement was short-lived, for that very evening news spread through the village that a young goat had vanished from a pen on the edge of town. By the following morning, a crowd of anxious herders had gathered outside the mosque, and the word on everyone's lips was "leopard." Some of the men spoke angrily of setting traps, while one even suggested leaving poisoned meat in the hills to deal with the problem once and for all. Abu Saad stood among them, nodding grimly, as if a prophecy he had made long ago had finally come true. Layla felt a cold knot tighten in her stomach. If the villagers acted on their anger, the last leopard of AlUla might be dead before anyone had even proved it existed.

Refusing to accept a hasty verdict, Layla persuaded her uncle to take her to the damaged pen, where she knelt down to scrutinise the ground. The earth was covered in prints, but something about them bothered her, and she pulled out her phone to compare them with the photograph of the leopard track. "Look," she said, pointing excitedly. "These prints show claw marks at the tip of every toe, but cats have retractable claws, so they usually leave no marks at all." Uncle Khalid knelt beside her, examined the tracks for a long moment and then let out a low whistle of admiration. "Dogs," he said slowly. "A pack of strays, most likely, coming down from the rubbish tip to scavenge for food." Layla knew, however, that evidence alone would not be enough to convince a village that had already made up its mind.

That night, after a great deal of persuasion, Abu Saad reluctantly agreed to join them on a stakeout near the goat pens, grumbling that he was far too old to sit on cold rocks chasing fairy tales. They wrapped themselves in thick blankets and waited in silence while the stars wheeled slowly above them, so bright and numerous that Layla felt she could almost reach up and gather them in her hands. Shortly after midnight, a series of shadows slipped out of the darkness and crept towards the pen. Uncle Khalid switched on his torch, and its beam revealed four scruffy, half-starved dogs that scattered, yelping, into the night. Abu Saad stared after them for a long time without speaking. "Well," he finally muttered, "it seems I owe somebody an apology, though I am not yet sure who."

They were packing up to leave when Layla froze, her hand gripping her grandfather's sleeve. High on the ridge above them, outlined against the pale glow of the rising moon, stood the unmistakable silhouette of a large cat, its long tail curling gently at the tip. For a few breathtaking seconds, the leopard gazed down at them, utterly still and utterly unafraid, before melting back into the rocks as silently as smoke. Nobody dared to breathe until it had gone. When Layla finally turned to her grandfather, she was astonished to see tears glistening in his eyes. "Sixty years," he whispered. "I had forgotten how beautiful they are."

The following afternoon, the camera trap beneath the overhanging rock delivered an even greater surprise: a clear image of a female leopard, followed closely by a small, wide-eyed cub. Uncle Khalid was so overjoyed that he phoned his colleagues in Riyadh three times before he had even finished his lunch. Yet it was Abu Saad who did the most important work that day. He walked into the gathering of herders, leaning on his cane, and told them plainly that the dogs, not the leopard, were to blame, and that anyone who laid poison in the hills would answer to him personally. Because he had once been the leopard's fiercest critic, the villagers listened to him in a way they would never have listened to a ranger or a teenage girl. By evening, the talk of traps had died away, replaced by plans to build stronger pens and to work with the authorities to deal with the stray dogs humanely.

On her last morning, Layla sat with her grandfather on the flat roof of his house, watching the sunrise paint the cliffs in shades of gold and rose. He asked to see the photograph of the cub once more and studied it with the tenderness he usually reserved for his grandchildren. "We should give him a name," he said thoughtfully, "something that reminds us he belongs to this land as much as we do." After some debate, they settled on Amal, meaning hope, because that was precisely what the little leopard had brought back to the valley. Layla had arrived in AlUla merely curious, but she was leaving with a clear sense of purpose: one day, she decided, she would study wildlife biology and return to protect these mountains herself. As the car pulled away, she glanced up at the ridge, half-convinced that somewhere among the rocks, a pair of golden eyes was watching her go.
