pages.text: Every night for almost two years, Faris had climbed onto the flat roof of his grandfather's house on the edge of AlUla, switched on his battered radio receiver, and listened to a satellite that everyone else had given up on. It was called Sadeem, and it had been built by his older sister Noura and her university engineering team, a box of circuits no larger than a loaf of bread. Three weeks after its launch, it had fallen silent without warning, and the team had reluctantly declared it lost. Noura had moved on to other projects, as engineers must, but Faris could not quite bring himself to let it go. He knew perfectly well that the odds of hearing from it again were next to nothing. Still, there was something about the stillness of the desert at night, with the sandstone cliffs glowing faintly under the stars, that made giving up feel like a betrayal.

On that particular night in late October, the air was cool enough that he had wrapped himself in his grandfather's old woollen shawl. He was half-asleep, lulled by the soft hiss of static, when a sound cut through it so faintly that at first he assumed he had imagined it. It was a rhythmic chirp, rising and falling, like a cricket calling from very far away. Faris sat bolt upright, his heart hammering, and pressed the headphones tightly against his ears. The chirp came again, then again, each pulse slightly higher in pitch than the last. He had read about this phenomenon a hundred times, but hearing it with his own ears was something else entirely: the signal was changing because its source was racing across the sky at nearly eight kilometres per second.

With trembling fingers, he connected the receiver to his laptop and let the decoding software do its work. Lines of characters scrolled across the screen, most of them meaningless, until one word appeared that made him catch his breath. SADEEM. Underneath it were numbers he only half understood: battery voltage, temperature, something labelled "spin rate" that looked alarmingly high. Faris stared at the screen for a long moment, unable to believe what he was seeing. Then, even though it was nearly two o'clock in the morning, he picked up his phone and called his sister.

"Faris, do you have any idea what time it is?" Noura mumbled, her voice thick with sleep. "It's Sadeem," he said, and the silence on the other end lasted so long that he wondered whether she had hung up. When she finally spoke, she sounded wide awake. "Send me everything, right now," she said, and he could hear her scrambling for her laptop. A few minutes later she explained what she thought had happened: the battery must have drained completely, and now that the satellite's orbit had shifted, sunlight was once again reaching its solar panels. "It's alive," she said quietly, "but it's tumbling out of control, and if we don't stabilise it soon, the battery will overheat and we'll lose it for good."

The problem, Noura went on, was one of timing rather than technology. The university's ground station in Riyadh would not have a clear view of the satellite for another four days, which would almost certainly be too late. However, according to her calculations, Sadeem would pass directly over AlUla at exactly 4:17 that morning, and it would remain above the horizon for just eleven minutes. "You have your amateur licence, and your antenna is better than you give it credit for," she said. "I'm going to send you a command sequence that should switch on its stabilisers. If you can transmit it at the right moment, there's a chance, a slim one, that it'll work." Faris swallowed hard, suddenly aware that a project years in the making might hinge on a homemade antenna and a seventeen-year-old's nerve.

At half past three, the roof door creaked open and his grandfather appeared, carrying a small tray with a flask of cardamom coffee and a plate of dates. "Your light has been on all night," he remarked mildly, settling himself on a cushion beside the antenna. Faris poured out the whole story in a rush, half expecting to be told to go to bed. Instead, the old man listened carefully and then gazed up at the sky, where the stars were scattered thickly across the darkness. "When I was a boy, we used the stars to find our way across the desert," he said. "Now you are trying to find your way to one of them. Breathe slowly, and do not let your hands run ahead of your head."

At 4:17 precisely, the faint chirp returned, and Faris transmitted the first command. Nothing happened. He tried again, then a third time, and still the satellite gave no sign that it had heard him. Four minutes had already slipped away, and he could feel panic creeping up his spine like a cold hand. Then, with a jolt, he remembered the rising pitch he had heard earlier: the satellite's movement was distorting the frequency, and he had forgotten to compensate for it. Forcing himself to slow down, exactly as his grandfather had advised, he began adjusting the dial by tiny increments, chasing the signal as it slid across the band.

With barely three minutes remaining, he sent the command once more. For several agonising seconds there was nothing but static, and Faris was convinced he had missed his chance. Then a new line of text blinked onto the screen: CMD RECEIVED. STABILISATION ACTIVE. He let out a shout that echoed off the nearby rooftops, and somewhere in the distance a dog began barking indignantly. His grandfather laughed and clapped him on the shoulder, while Noura, still on the phone, was practically shouting with relief. A moment later, the chirp faded into silence as Sadeem dipped below the horizon, carrying their hopes with it.

They would not know for certain whether the command had worked until the satellite's next pass, ninety minutes later, a brief seven-minute window just before dawn. Those ninety minutes felt longer than the previous two years combined. When the signal finally returned, it was noticeably stronger and steadier, and the spin rate had dropped to almost nothing. Then, to Faris's astonishment, the software began to receive something new: a small image, assembled painstakingly line by line as the data trickled in. It was blurry and low in resolution, but there was no mistaking it. Spread beneath the satellite lay the curve of the Red Sea coastline, the water glittering silver as the first rays of the rising sun touched it.

By mid-morning, the photograph had been shared with the entire engineering department, and Noura's professor, Dr. Hamdan, had phoned Faris personally. He wanted to know whether Faris would consider joining the university's ground station team over the summer, adding with a chuckle that they could clearly use someone with his patience. Faris accepted before the professor had even finished the sentence. That evening, as the sun sank behind the cliffs, he sat on the roof with his grandfather once more and watched the sky slowly darken. "Most people thought you were wasting your time up here," the old man said. "Perhaps," Faris replied, smiling as the first star appeared, "but sometimes the most important thing you can do is simply keep listening."

questions.q: Why could the university's ground station in Riyadh not help save Sadeem?
options: Its equipment had been damaged in a storm.
It would not have a clear view of the satellite for another four days.
Dr. Hamdan refused to give permission.

questions.q: What mistake did Faris make during his first attempts to send the command?
options: He forgot to compensate for the change in frequency caused by the satellite's movement.
He typed the command sequence incorrectly.
He pointed his antenna in the wrong direction.

questions.q: In the text, the phrase "might hinge on" a homemade antenna most nearly means:
options: might be damaged by
might depend on
might be replaced by

questions.q: What can we infer about the grandfather's character from the story?
options: He is impatient and dislikes modern technology.
He is worried that Faris is neglecting his studies.
He is calm, supportive and connects the past with the present.

questions.q: What is the main message of the story's ending?
options: Persistence and patience can be rewarded, even when others have given up.
Amateurs should leave space science to professionals.
Technology is more reliable than human judgement.

stories.title: The Loneliest Man on the Pitch

pages.text: Two years earlier, Faris Al-Harbi had been the fastest winger in his age group in the whole of the Eastern Province, a slim boy who could leave defenders stranded with a single drop of his shoulder. Then, in the final minutes of an ordinary training session, his knee had twisted beneath him with a sound he would never forget. The surgeon was kind but blunt: the ligament would heal, yet his days of playing at a competitive level were almost certainly over. For months afterwards, Faris could hardly bear to walk past a football pitch, let alone sit in the stands and watch his former teammates carry on without him. It felt, he told his mother, like being exiled from the only country he had ever wanted to live in. It was his Uncle Saleh, a retired referee with a voice like gravel and a habit of quoting the Laws of the Game at dinner, who finally offered him a way back.

The refereeing course turned out to be far more demanding than Faris had anticipated. There were evenings spent memorising obscure regulations about dropped balls and encroachment, and mornings spent sprinting between cones until his lungs burned. More challenging still were his first real matches, where parents bellowed from the touchline as though he had personally insulted their families. "A referee is invisible when he is right and unforgettable when he is wrong," Uncle Saleh reminded him after one particularly bruising afternoon. Gradually, however, Faris discovered that he possessed an unexpected gift for reading the game. Years as a winger had taught him exactly how attackers thought, where they would run, and, crucially, when they were tempted to cheat.

So when the regional federation appointed him to officiate the Under-17 Cup final, Faris was thrilled for roughly ten seconds, until he read the names of the two teams. One of them was Al-Nakheel, his old club, coached by Abu Hamad, the man who had first spotted him kicking a ball against a mosque wall at the age of eight. Its captain was Yousef, his closest friend since primary school. Faris knew that the honourable thing was to declare the conflict of interest, even if it cost him the biggest match of his young career. The assessor, Mr. Al-Qahtani, listened gravely, made a phone call, and then explained that no other qualified referee was available at such short notice. "We are keeping you," he said, fixing Faris with a steady gaze, "because you were honest enough to tell us, and I expect that honesty to last for ninety minutes."

The final was played on a humid evening under blazing floodlights, with families packed into the stands and the scent of cardamom coffee drifting from flasks passed along the rows. As the captains met in the centre circle, Yousef grinned and murmured, "Go easy on us, brother." Faris kept his expression neutral and simply asked him to call heads or tails, though inwardly the words stung more than he cared to admit. The match was ferociously contested from the first whistle, with tackles flying in and tempers simmering just beneath the surface. Al-Nakheel took the lead through a deflected free kick, only for their opponents, Al-Shorouq, to equalise with a superb header shortly after half-time. By the closing stages, the score stood at one each, and every player on the pitch looked as though he were running on nothing but willpower.

In the eighty-eighth minute, Yousef collected a loose ball, burst into the penalty area and tumbled to the ground as a defender slid towards him. The crowd erupted, hundreds of voices demanding a penalty in one deafening roar. Faris, however, had been perfectly positioned, barely ten metres away, and he had seen something that nobody in the stands could possibly have noticed. The defender had pulled his leg away at the last moment, and Yousef, anticipating contact that never came, had deliberately left his trailing foot to catch the grass. Time seemed to slow almost to a standstill as Faris's heart hammered against his ribs. He knew precisely what the correct decision was, and he knew just as precisely what it would cost him.

Faris blew his whistle, waved away the appeals for a penalty and, with a hand that trembled only slightly, showed Yousef a yellow card for simulation. For a moment there was stunned silence, and then the Al-Nakheel supporters unleashed a storm of jeers. Yousef stared at him in disbelief, his face flushed with something between anger and shame. On the touchline, Abu Hamad flung his arms in the air and shouted, "You, of all people, Faris! After everything!" Faris turned away and restarted play, refusing to let the noise penetrate the calm he had spent two years building. Inside, though, he felt as if the ground beneath him had begun to crumble.

The match ended level, and Al-Nakheel went on to lose the penalty shootout after their third kick struck the crossbar and bounced harmlessly away. As Faris walked towards the tunnel, a chorus of whistles followed him, and a half-empty water bottle landed at his feet. Nobody congratulated him; nobody even looked at him, apart from those glaring with open hostility. Alone in the cramped changing room, he sat with his head in his hands and replayed the incident over and over in his mind. What if he had been mistaken? What if a single flawed judgement had destroyed his friendship, his reputation and the dreams of an entire team in one cruel instant?

It was Uncle Saleh who eventually knocked on the door, holding up his phone with an air of quiet satisfaction. A spectator had filmed the incident from behind the goal, and the slow-motion footage, which was already circulating widely online, left no room whatsoever for doubt. The defender had never touched Yousef, and the dive was as clear as daylight. "You did not see it from the stands, Faris; you saw it from the place where a referee is supposed to be," his uncle said, resting a weathered hand on his shoulder. "In this job, your reward is rarely applause, and sometimes it is only the knowledge that you have been fair." Faris let out a long breath, though he suspected that knowledge alone would not mend what had been broken that evening.

The following afternoon, the doorbell rang, and Faris opened it to find Yousef standing awkwardly on the step, his eyes fixed firmly on his trainers. Over glasses of mint tea in the majlis, his friend confessed that a scout from a professional academy had been in the stands, and that in a moment of panic he had thrown himself to the ground without really thinking. "I wanted it so badly that I forgot who I was," he admitted, his voice barely above a whisper. He added that Abu Hamad had watched the footage late into the night and was too ashamed to face Faris just yet. "He asked me to tell you something, though," Yousef said with a faint smile. "He said he taught you to play football, but apparently you have just taught him what it is for."

Three weeks later, a letter arrived from the national federation, inviting Faris to join its elite panel of young referees, citing the assessor's glowing report on his conduct under pressure. That same evening, Abu Hamad appeared at the house in person, embraced him warmly and apologised before Faris could utter a single word. Weeks afterwards, as the sun dipped behind the palm trees, Faris and Yousef kicked a ball around the old neighbourhood pitch, carefully, gently, for the sheer joy of it rather than for any trophy. Yousef, who had since been offered a trial on merit alone, joked that he would never dare fall over again while Faris was within a hundred kilometres. Faris laughed and tossed him the ball, realising that he had not lost football after all; he had simply found a different way to love it. The loneliest man on the pitch, he now understood, was never truly alone, provided he could live with every decision he made.

questions.q: Why did the assessor decide to keep Faris as the referee for the final?
options: No other qualified referee was available, and Faris had been honest about the conflict
Faris's uncle asked the federation to give him the match
Al-Nakheel's coach specifically requested Faris

questions.q: What did Faris actually see when Yousef fell in the penalty area?
options: The defender tripped Yousef with a late tackle
The defender pulled his leg away, and Yousef deliberately caught his own foot on the grass
Yousef slipped accidentally on the wet pitch

questions.q: In the story, what does the word 'simulation' mean?
options: A computer training exercise for referees
Pretending to be fouled in order to win a decision
A tactic used to waste time

questions.q: Why did Yousef dive, according to his confession?
options: Abu Hamad had told him to try to win a penalty
He was injured and could not keep running
He panicked because a scout from a professional academy was watching

questions.q: What does Abu Hamad's message, 'you have just taught him what it is for', suggest?
options: He now realises that fairness and integrity matter more than winning
He wants Faris to become a coach instead of a referee
He believes the referee should have awarded the penalty

pages.text: Uncle Mansour was a man who laminated his shopping lists, and everyone in the Al-Harbi family knew it. So when he chose sixteen-year-old Yusuf to send the invitation for Grandmother's eightieth birthday, the honour felt suspiciously like a test. "The family group has one hundred and forty-three members," Uncle Mansour said gravely, standing over him in the majlis. "In nine years, I have never once posted a spelling mistake there, and I do not intend to begin now." He dictated the message slowly, pausing between phrases as though he were carving them into stone. Yusuf nodded, promised to send it that evening, and assured his uncle that nothing could possibly go wrong.

Unfortunately, that evening Yusuf was also helping his mother stuff vine leaves, so he typed the message with one sticky thumb while she called out instructions from the stove. His phone, which had been trained by years of late-night gaming chats, had developed opinions of its own about the English language. Without rereading a single word, he pressed send and went back to the vine leaves. It was only when his phone began buzzing like a trapped wasp that he glanced at the screen. The message read: "Grandmother's eightieth birthday will be held on Friday after Asr. Please bring your appliances. Uncle Mansour will deliver a short sheep." Two blue ticks had already appeared, and the damage, as they say, was done.

The replies arrived faster than Yusuf could read them. Aunt Noura asked, with apparent sincerity, whether a spare blender would be acceptable or whether something larger was expected. Cousin Tariq wanted to know if the sheep was coming from Uncle Mansour's farm and whether it had been rehearsing. Yusuf's face burned as he typed a correction, this time slowly and with both hands. "Apologies, I meant SPEECH, not sheep, and please don't bring appliances, just appetites." He pressed send with enormous relief, only to watch, frozen in horror, as the final word quietly transformed itself into "apricots."

By now the family had decided that the birthday must have a theme, and the theme was clearly apricots. Great-Uncle Saad, who was ninety and rarely used his phone, recorded a four-minute voice note about the extraordinary apricots of Taif in 1962. Determined not to dig himself any deeper, Yusuf locked himself in the bathroom to record a calm, clear explanation. Halfway through, however, his little sister Lulwa switched on the vacuum cleaner right outside the door. When he played the recording back, the only words that could be heard above the roar were "sheep," "Friday," and "everyone must." He deleted it, sat on the edge of the bathtub, and wondered whether it was too late to move to another country.

At ten o'clock his phone rang, and the name on the screen made his stomach drop: Uncle Mansour. For a long moment, there was nothing on the line but slow, deliberate breathing. "Yusuf," his uncle said at last, "I have just received three messages asking what size my sheep is." Yusuf began a rambling apology about autocorrect, vine leaves and the vacuum cleaner, but his uncle cut him short. "Fix it by Thursday," he said, and hung up without another word. Yusuf spent the next two days sending increasingly desperate clarifications, each of which, somehow, only made matters worse.

On Friday afternoon, the relatives began to arrive, and Yusuf watched from the doorway with a sinking heart. Aunt Noura marched in carrying her blender like a trophy, followed by a cousin clutching a brand-new air fryer still in its box. Crates of apricots appeared in the hallway until it smelled like an orchard in midsummer. Then Cousin Tariq strolled in, grinning from ear to ear, leading a small, fluffy lamb on a rope. "Borrowed it from the farm," he announced proudly. "I didn't want Uncle Mansour to be embarrassed if his sheep failed to turn up."

What followed could only be described as organised chaos. Aunt Noura plugged in her blender and began producing apricot juice for anyone who stood still long enough. The children discovered that the air fryer made surprisingly good apricot pastries, and soon a small, sticky industry was under way in the kitchen. Meanwhile, the lamb wandered freely through the majlis, inspecting cushions and politely ignoring every attempt to catch it. Just as Uncle Mansour rose to deliver his speech, the lamb trotted past, seized his laminated notes between its teeth, and chewed them with an expression of deep satisfaction. The room fell completely silent, apart from the steady, crunching sound of plastic.

Uncle Mansour stared at his empty hands as if he had never seen them before. For the first time anyone could remember, he had nothing prepared, and Yusuf was certain he was about to witness a disaster. Instead, his uncle cleared his throat and began, hesitantly at first, to talk about his mother. He spoke about the nights she had stayed awake when he was ill as a boy, and the way she still slipped sweets into his pocket even though he was fifty-two. By the time he finished, several of the aunts were dabbing their eyes, and even Great-Uncle Saad had stopped talking about 1962. It was, everyone agreed afterwards, the best speech he had ever given, precisely because he had not written it.

Grandmother, who had been watching everything from her favourite chair, suddenly began to laugh so hard that her shoulders shook. "Eighty years," she said, wiping her eyes, "and every birthday has been exactly the same, until today." Then she told them something none of them had known. As a little girl in Taif, she had climbed her father's apricot trees every summer, and no fruit in the world had ever tasted as sweet. "I have not seen this many apricots in one place since I was nine," she said, beaming at Yusuf. "Whoever wrote that invitation deserves a reward." Yusuf, who had spent all week expecting a punishment, didn't quite know what to do with his face.

Later that night, after the lamb had been returned, the appliances packed away and the last apricot eaten, Yusuf's phone buzzed once more. It was a message in the family group from Uncle Mansour, and Yusuf opened it with a mixture of curiosity and dread. "Thank you all for coming to celebrate our mother," it read. "It was truly a memorable sheep." A full minute passed before a second message appeared: "EVENING. I meant EVENING." Within seconds, one hundred and forty-two laughing faces flooded the chat, and Yusuf laughed until his sides ached. Some mistakes, he decided, were simply too good to correct.

questions.q: Why did Yusuf's first message contain so many mistakes?
options: He typed quickly with one sticky thumb and didn't reread it before sending
Uncle Mansour dictated the wrong words to him on purpose
His little sister Lulwa secretly changed the message

questions.q: In the phrase "the damage, as they say, was done," what does the writer mean?
options: Yusuf's phone had been physically broken
It was too late to undo the mistake because people had already seen it
Uncle Mansour had already punished Yusuf

questions.q: What happened to Uncle Mansour's speech notes?
options: He left them at home on his farm
Aunt Noura accidentally put them in the blender
The lamb chewed them just before he began speaking

questions.q: Why was Uncle Mansour's speech considered his best ever?
options: Because it was the shortest speech he had ever given
Because he spoke honestly from the heart instead of reading prepared notes
Because Yusuf helped him rewrite it at the last minute

questions.q: What can we infer from Uncle Mansour's final message in the family group?
options: Even a careful person like him can make autocorrect mistakes, which makes the ending ironic
He was still angry with Yusuf and wanted to embarrass him
He had decided to leave the family group forever

stories.title: The Boy Who Caught the Clouds

pages.text: Every morning, without fail, the fog came to the village of Al-Sawda, rolling over the peaks of the Asir mountains like a slow white tide. It wrapped itself around the stone houses, swallowed the narrow roads and settled on the terraced fields that Faisal's grandfather had tended for over fifty years. Yet by midday it had always vanished, leaving behind nothing but the same cracked earth and the same thirsty pomegranate trees. The rains had been unreliable for three seasons now, and the wells were lower than anyone could remember. "The mountain is surrounded by water," his grandfather remarked one morning, gazing at the mist with a bitter smile, "and still it dies of thirst." Faisal, who was seventeen and rarely took anything at face value, could not get those words out of his head.

That night, while the rest of the house slept, he sat hunched over his laptop, reading everything he could find about fog. He discovered that in the deserts of Chile and Morocco, villagers had strung up enormous mesh nets that harvested tiny droplets from the passing mist, turning clouds into drinking water. The principle was surprisingly simple: as fog drifts through a fine net, water condenses on the fibres, gathers into drops and trickles down into a gutter below. By the time the call to Fajr prayer drifted across the valley, Faisal had filled six pages of his notebook with sketches and calculations. His younger sister Noura found him at breakfast, red-eyed but grinning. "You look like you've either solved something or lost your mind," she observed, pouring herself some tea.

His first prototype was, to put it kindly, a makeshift affair: a sheet of green mosquito netting stretched between two broom handles, with a split plastic pipe beneath it to catch the runoff. Noura, sceptical but curious, helped him wedge it between the rocks on the north edge of the highest terrace. The next morning they raced up the slope before dawn, only to find that the bucket contained barely enough water to fill a teacup. Faisal stared at it, crushed, while his sister tactfully pretended to examine a beetle on the wall. Their grandfather wandered up behind them, peered into the bucket and nodded gravely. "Excellent," he said. "At this rate, my trees will be watered in about four hundred years."

Despite the setback, Faisal was determined not to throw in the towel, especially since the regional science and innovation fair in Abha was only five weeks away. His physics teacher, Mr Al-Ghamdi, listened to the whole saga with genuine interest and then asked a question that stopped him in his tracks. "You've copied the net," he said, "but have you understood why it works, or why yours doesn't?" Faisal had to admit that he had been so eager to build something that he had skipped the painstaking business of actually experimenting. To make matters worse, word had spread that a student from Riyadh was entering the fair with an autonomous drone that could map crop diseases from the air. Next to that, a dripping mosquito net seemed almost embarrassing.

The breakthrough came from the most unexpected place. One foggy afternoon, Noura left her grandmother's old palm-leaf basket on the courtyard wall, and when she went to fetch it, she found it glistening with beads of water. Faisal crouched beside it, fascinated, noticing that the drops clung most heavily wherever the weave was thick and knotted, then slid neatly along the grooves to the base. "It's not just about the material," he murmured, almost to himself. "It's the texture, the shape, the way the water is guided." Their grandfather, overhearing, mentioned that the old farmers had always built their walls angled towards the north, precisely because the stones there stayed damp the longest. For the first time in weeks, the pieces began to fall into place.

Over the following fortnight, Faisal transformed the garage into a workshop, testing dozens of fabrics, knots and angles with the dedication of a scientist and the stubbornness of a mountain goat. He measured every drop, recorded the wind direction each morning and gradually designed a three-dimensional mesh inspired by the basket's pattern, with tiny ridges that channelled the water downward before the wind could blow it away. Noura became his unofficial assistant, though she insisted on the title "co-inventor" and made him write it on the project poster. By the final week, the new collector was gathering almost two litres a night, more than fifty times as much as the first attempt. Faisal had never felt so proud of anything in his life. Then, two nights before the fair, the storm arrived.

It howled across the mountains for hours, rattling the shutters and bending the old trees almost to the ground. At first light, Faisal ran outside and found his collector lying in a crumpled heap against the terrace wall, its frame snapped in two and its carefully woven mesh torn to shreds. He sank down onto the wet stones, unable to speak, as all those weeks of effort seemed to dissolve before his eyes. His grandfather sat beside him in silence for a long while before finally placing a weathered hand on his shoulder. "An invention that cannot survive the mountain," he said gently, "is not yet finished." Faisal looked up and, slowly, realised that this was not the end of the project but simply its next chapter.

Rather than building a rigid frame that fought against the wind, Faisal decided to design one that would yield to it, just as the palm trees in the courtyard had swayed through the storm without breaking. Working almost without rest, he salvaged what he could from the wreckage and built a new frame from flexible fibreglass rods that bent under pressure and sprang back afterwards. Noura re-wove the damaged sections of mesh while their mother kept them supplied with dates, coffee and firm reminders to pray on time and sleep at least a little. Even their grandfather, who claimed to know nothing about technology, turned out to be remarkably good at tying knots. By the time they loaded the collector into the car, it was scratched, patched and far from beautiful. But it was stronger than anything Faisal had built before.

At the fair, the exhibition hall was full of gleaming robots and glowing screens, and the judges' first glance at Faisal's patched contraption was distinctly unenthusiastic. Worse still, there was no fog indoors to demonstrate how it worked. Thinking on his feet, Faisal borrowed a steaming urn of Arabic coffee from the refreshments table, positioned it beneath the mesh and, to the delight of the gathering crowd, the fabric soon began to sparkle with droplets that ran neatly into the gutter. He then explained the storm, the basket and the flexible frame, speaking not like someone reciting a speech but like someone who had lived every moment of it. When the results were announced, the drone from Riyadh took first place, and Faisal came second. Afterwards, the drone's inventor shook his hand and admitted, with a laugh, that he would never look at a cup of coffee in the same way again.

A week later, the fog returned to Al-Sawda as it always had, drifting silently over the terraces before dawn. This time, however, three of Faisal's collectors stood waiting on the north ridge, their flexible frames swaying gently as the mist passed through them. When the sun finally rose, the water tank beneath them held more than five litres of clear, cold water. Their grandfather filled a jug, walked slowly to the oldest pomegranate tree and poured it carefully around the roots, murmuring a quiet prayer of thanks. "So," he said, turning to his grandchildren with a twinkle in his eye, "it seems the mountain can drink after all." That evening, Faisal opened a fresh page in his notebook and wrote two words at the top: Version Four.

questions.q: Why did Faisal's first fog collector fail?
options: He had copied the idea without experimenting or understanding why it worked
The fog never reached the north terrace
His sister accidentally damaged the net

questions.q: What gave Faisal the idea for his improved mesh design?
options: A drone he saw at the science fair
Water collecting on his grandmother's palm-leaf basket
A video his teacher showed in class

questions.q: In the story, the phrase "throw in the towel" means:
options: to clean up after a mistake
to give up
to start a new project

questions.q: What lesson did the storm and his grandfather's words teach Faisal?
options: That fog collection is impossible in the mountains
That he should design something that works with nature's forces, not against them
That he should copy the drone instead

questions.q: What does the final line, "Version Four," suggest about Faisal?
options: He is disappointed that he only came second
He has decided to stop inventing
He sees invention as a continuous process of improvement

stories.title: The Robot That Refused to Behave

pages.text: The solar farm stretched across the plain east of Tabuk like a sea of black glass, thousands of panels tilted towards a sun that showed no mercy. Yusuf had arrived for a summer placement arranged by his uncle Khalid, the site's chief engineer, expecting six weeks of tedious paperwork and lukewarm tea. Instead, he had been put in charge of something he found far more intriguing: the fleet of cleaning robots that crawled along the rows each night, brushing away the dust that could cut the panels' output by a third. There were ninety-six of them, squat and tireless, each one following a route calculated to the centimetre. Ninety-five behaved impeccably. The ninety-sixth, officially designated Unit 23, had developed what the technicians politely called "a personality problem."

Every night for a fortnight, Unit 23 had abandoned its assigned row at precisely the same point, swerved into the open sand beyond the fence, and traced a long, wandering line before returning to work as if nothing had happened. "It's a software glitch, plain and simple," said Majed, a senior technician who had little patience for machines with ideas of their own. "We wipe its memory, reinstall the system, and the problem disappears." Yusuf, however, had been studying the GPS logs, and something about them nagged at him. The line the robot drew was never random; it was identical every single night, down to the smallest curve. Glitches, in his experience, were rarely so consistent. He asked his uncle for three days to investigate, and Khalid, amused by his nephew's determination, reluctantly agreed.

Yusuf spent the first evening buried in the robot's diagnostic data, his laptop balanced on a crate in the maintenance shed. Unit 23, he discovered, was one of a handful of newer models fitted with ground-penetrating sensors, intended to detect weak soil before the robots drove onto it. According to the readings, the robot was not wandering at all; it was carefully skirting around something beneath the surface. A narrow band of the ground below registered as hollow, a void running for nearly half a kilometre beneath the sand. "So it isn't disobeying," Yusuf murmured to himself, "it's avoiding danger." The trouble was that the hollow band cut directly beneath row forty-one, which, according to the robot's programming, it had every reason to fear.

The question of what lay underground kept Yusuf awake long after the generators had fallen silent. Scrolling through old regional surveys on his phone, he stumbled upon a reference that made him sit bolt upright. For centuries, communities across Arabia had built underground water channels, sometimes called aflaj, which carried water from distant aquifers to farms and settlements without losing it to evaporation. Many had been forgotten as wells and pipelines replaced them, their entrances buried by shifting dunes. If one of those channels ran beneath the solar farm, it would explain everything: the hollow readings, the unwavering path, the robot's apparent stubbornness. It would also mean that row forty-one had been built on top of a tunnel nobody knew existed.

The next morning, Yusuf presented his findings to the engineering team, his voice steadier than he felt. Majed folded his arms and listened with an expression that suggested he was being made to watch a rather silly film. "With respect," he said once Yusuf had finished, "you're building an entire theory on the behaviour of a faulty robot. Sensors misread soil all the time, especially when it's been baked like this." A few of the others nodded, and Yusuf felt his confidence begin to crumble. Khalid, however, rubbed his beard thoughtfully and pointed out that the heavy maintenance truck was scheduled to drive down row forty-one that very afternoon to replace a damaged inverter. "If the boy is right," he said quietly, "that truck weighs eleven tonnes."

Before anyone could decide what to do, the sky to the west turned an ominous shade of ochre. A sandstorm was rolling in faster than the forecast had predicted, and in the confusion of securing equipment, the truck driver, who had missed the meeting, set off early to finish the job before visibility vanished. Yusuf only realised what was happening when he saw the vehicle's headlights swing towards row forty-one through the thickening haze. He grabbed a radio, but the channel crackled uselessly with static. Then, to his astonishment, he noticed a small shape trundling across the sand ahead of the truck. Unit 23 had left its charging dock without instructions and positioned itself squarely in the vehicle's path.

The truck's collision sensors registered the obstacle, and it ground to a halt barely two metres from the little robot. Yusuf sprinted through the stinging sand, his scarf pulled over his mouth, and hammered on the driver's window until the startled man lowered it. "Don't go any further," he gasped, "the ground here might not hold you." The driver looked at him as though he had taken leave of his senses, but something in Yusuf's face persuaded him to reverse. Moments later, as the truck crawled backwards, a section of sand just ahead of where its front wheels had been sagged and then slid inwards with a soft, sinister hiss. A dark opening yawned in the desert floor, and the wind began pouring sand into it like water down a drain.

When the storm finally blew itself out that evening, the entire team gathered around the hole with torches and a sense of quiet disbelief. Below them, perhaps four metres down, ran a tunnel lined with carefully fitted stones, its curved roof still largely intact after what must have been centuries. Majed crouched at the edge for a long time without speaking. At last he straightened up, brushed the dust from his knees, and turned to Yusuf with a rueful smile. "I owe you an apology," he admitted, "and I suppose I owe that robot one too." Yusuf laughed, partly from relief, and partly because he had never heard anyone apologise to a machine before.

Within a week, a team of archaeologists from the Heritage Commission had arrived, and the solar farm found itself unexpectedly in the news. The specialists confirmed that the channel was part of an ancient water system, possibly more than a thousand years old, which had once fed a settlement whose ruins lay buried a few kilometres away. Row forty-one was dismantled and rebuilt on safer ground, and the company agreed to protect the tunnel as a site of historical importance. One archaeologist, an elderly professor with a gentle voice, asked to see the robot that had made the discovery. She studied Unit 23's sensor maps with the delight of someone handed a treasure map, and declared that they were more accurate than anything her team could have produced in a month.

On the last evening of his placement, Yusuf sat on the warm sand beside Unit 23 and watched the sun sink behind the endless rows of panels. Nobody talked about wiping its memory any more; instead, the engineers had begun discussing how its sensors might be used to survey other sites across the region. Yusuf had arrived thinking he wanted to be an engineer, but now he found himself wondering whether he might also study archaeology, and whether the two might somehow fit together. His uncle joined him and handed him a cup of cardamom coffee, its fragrance drifting on the cooling air. "You know what the real lesson is?" Khalid said. "Sometimes the one who refuses to follow the line is the only one paying attention." Unit 23 blinked its small green light, as if it entirely agreed.

pages.text: In the spring of 1908, the newest thing in the northern Hijaz was not a building or a market but a line of iron stretching across the desert as far as the eye could see. Sixteen-year-old Yusuf had been taken on as an apprentice at a small stone station near the ancient tombs of Hegra, and he had never been prouder of anything in his life. Every morning he polished the brass of the telegraph machine until it gleamed, and every afternoon he practised tapping out messages in Morse code under the patient eye of the station master, Saleh. The railway was meant to carry pilgrims from Damascus to Medina in days rather than weeks, and Yusuf felt as though he were standing at the very edge of history. To him, the clicking of the telegraph was the sound of the future arriving.

His father, Hamad, saw things rather differently. For thirty years he had guided caravans through these valleys, reading the land the way other men read books, and he regarded the railway with deep suspicion. "Iron cannot read the sky," he would say, watching the smoke of a passing engine with narrowed eyes. "A camel knows when a storm is coming; does your machine?" Yusuf usually bit his tongue, but one evening he could hold back no longer. "Father, the world is changing whether we like it or not," he said, more sharply than he had intended. Hamad said nothing, but the silence that followed weighed on both of them for days.

Late one afternoon, towards the end of the week, the air grew strangely heavy and still. Hamad, who had come to the station with fresh bread, stopped in the doorway and studied the dark wall of cloud building over the mountains to the north. "Rain is falling up there, and plenty of it," he murmured. "By nightfall, every wadi between here and Tabuk will be running like a river." Saleh, who had been suffering from a fever all day, waved the warning away from his bed in the back room, insisting that the stone bridges had been built by the finest engineers in the empire. Yet Yusuf noticed that his father did not go home that evening; instead, he sat by the window, saying his prayers and keeping a quiet watch on the horizon.

The storm broke just after sunset, and it was unlike anything Yusuf had ever witnessed. Rain hammered the roof so violently that conversation became impossible, and within an hour a roar like distant thunder rose from the valley north of the station. When the rain eased, Yusuf took a lantern and walked along the track as far as Wadi al-Hajar, where a stone bridge carried the line over a usually dry riverbed. What he saw made his heart sink: the floodwater had torn away the earth beneath one end of the bridge, leaving the rails hanging over empty space. He ran back to the station and seized the telegraph key, but the machine was dead, its line almost certainly brought down by the storm. According to the timetable, the night train from the north, packed with pilgrims bound for Medina, was due in less than two hours.

Saleh, burning with fever, could barely sit up, let alone walk. "The train must be stopped before it reaches the bridge," he whispered, "and that means someone has to get to the other side of the wadi." Yusuf stared at him in dismay, because the bridge was impassable and the flood was far too fierce to cross on foot. It was then that his father rose from his place by the window and calmly wrapped his cloak around his shoulders. "There is a narrow place upstream, where the rocks rise out of the riverbed," Hamad said. "I have crossed it many times, though never at night, and never in a flood like this one." He looked at his son, and for the first time in weeks there was no disagreement between them at all.

They rode out on Hamad's old camel, Yusuf clutching the station's red signal lantern against his chest. The moon slipped in and out of the clouds, and the noise of the water grew louder until it seemed to fill the whole world. At the crossing, Hamad dismounted and led the animal forward step by step, testing every stone with his staff before trusting it with their weight. Twice the camel stumbled, and once a surge of muddy water rose almost to Yusuf's knees, threatening to sweep them both downstream. "Don't look at the water; look at the far bank," his father called over the roar, and Yusuf held on for dear life. When at last they scrambled up onto solid ground, both of them were soaked to the skin, but they had made it.

They hurried north along the track until, far away, a single golden light appeared and began to grow. Yusuf lifted the red lantern high above his head and swung it from side to side, exactly as Saleh had taught him. Then, at the worst possible moment, a gust of wind snuffed out the flame, plunging them into darkness. With trembling fingers, Yusuf felt in his pocket for the matches, fully expecting them to be ruined by the flood. To his astonishment, they were perfectly dry, wrapped in a scrap of oiled leather, because his father had insisted, years earlier, that a traveller should never carry fire without protecting it. The flame caught, the red glow blazed once more, and with a long, piercing shriek of brakes, the great engine shuddered to a halt barely a hundred metres from where they stood.

The driver, a broad-shouldered man from Damascus, jumped down from his cabin, ready to demand an explanation. When Yusuf led him forward and he saw, by the light of his own lamp, the rails dangling over the black, rushing water, the colour drained from his face. "Another minute," he said quietly, "and none of us would have lived to see the morning." Word spread quickly through the carriages, and soon pilgrims were stepping down into the cool night air, many of them raising their hands in prayer and giving thanks to God. An elderly man from Aleppo took Yusuf's hand in both of his own and refused to let go for a long time. Yusuf, who had never felt so exhausted or so grateful, could hardly find the words to reply.

By the following afternoon, a repair crew had arrived, and the passengers were carried safely around the damaged bridge by a long line of camels that Hamad had gathered from the nearby villages. Saleh, his fever finally breaking, insisted on writing a full report so that the railway officials would know exactly what had happened. As father and son walked home together that evening, Yusuf finally said what had been on his mind all day. "You were right, Father; the machine could not read the sky." Hamad smiled and shook his head slowly. "And I could not have stopped that train without your lantern," he replied. "Perhaps the old ways and the new ones are meant to travel side by side."

More than a century later, a group of students stood in a restored station building near Al-Ula, listening to their guide describe the history of the Hijaz Railway. In a glass case before them lay a battered red lantern, its paint faded, beside a small scrap of dark, oiled leather. "These belonged to a young apprentice named Yusuf," the guide explained, "and to his father, who knew this desert better than any map." One of the students, a girl with sharp, curious eyes, leaned closer to read the label, then smiled to herself, because the name of her own great-great-grandfather was written there. Outside, the old rails still ran across the sand towards Medina, silent now but far from forgotten. And somewhere in the distance, as if the land itself remembered, the wind carried the faint promise of rain.

pages.text: When Faisal's parents announced that he would be spending the summer with his grandfather in the mountains north-west of AlUla, he had greeted the news with barely concealed dismay. Life in Riyadh, with its air-conditioned malls and endless chats with friends, seemed a far cry from a stone house at the edge of a silent wadi. His grandfather, Abu Saleh, had been a shepherd for most of his life, and he spoke about the land as though it were an old friend with moods and secrets. On Faisal's very first evening, as they drank sweet tea beneath a sky crowded with stars, the old man leaned forward and lowered his voice. "The nimr has come back," he said. "I have seen its tracks near the old well, and they were not there last spring." Faisal, who knew that the Arabian leopard had not been reliably recorded in the wild there for decades, smiled politely and decided to take the story with a pinch of salt.

Two days later, a dusty white pickup rattled up the track, and a young ranger named Majid climbed out, brushing sand from his uniform. He worked for a conservation programme that was preparing, in the years to come, to return captive-bred leopards to these very mountains. "Your grandfather called me," he explained to Faisal, shaking his hand warmly. "Honestly, we get reports like this every few months, and almost all of them turn out to be caracals or large foxes." Abu Saleh, far from being offended, simply nodded as if he had expected nothing less. "Then lend us your cameras," he replied calmly, "and let the mountain answer for itself." Majid hesitated, glanced at the old man's steady expression, and then fetched three camera traps from the back of the truck.

They set out before dawn, while the rocks still held the coolness of the night and the eastern sky was turning the colour of apricots. Faisal had assumed they would simply fix the cameras wherever the view was best, but his grandfather had other ideas. He paused at narrow passes between boulders, examined scratches on the bark of an acacia, and crouched to study droppings that Faisal would never have noticed. "A leopard is a creature of habit," Abu Saleh murmured. "It walks the same paths its mother walked, just as we do." Majid, who had a university degree in zoology, watched the old man with growing respect and quietly adjusted the angle of each camera to match his advice. By the time the sun had cleared the ridge, all three devices were strapped to rocks and hidden among the scrub.

For the next ten days, they collected the memory cards every second morning and scrolled through hundreds of images on Majid's laptop. The cameras had captured a remarkable parade of wildlife: red foxes trotting past at midnight, a family of Nubian ibex picking their way down the cliffs, and even a caracal with its tufted black ears. Had he seen such pictures a month earlier, Faisal would have been thrilled, but now each one felt like a small defeat. "We're looking for a needle in a haystack," he complained, slumping back in his chair. His grandfather merely poured him another cup of tea. "The desert does not hurry for anyone," he said, "and it certainly will not hurry for a boy from Riyadh."

On the eleventh afternoon, unable to bear the waiting any longer, Faisal did something he would later regret. Although he had promised never to walk into the hills alone, he slipped out while his grandfather was resting and headed towards the furthest camera. Near the old well, the sand was soft, and there, pressed clearly into its surface, were four rounded pads and no sign of claws, prints far too large to belong to any fox. His heart began to pound so loudly that he could almost hear it echoing off the rocks. Then, from somewhere above him, came a strange, rasping sound, like a saw being dragged slowly through wood. Faisal froze, suddenly aware that the sun had slipped behind the mountains and that the shadows were deepening around him at an alarming speed.

By the time he had retraced his steps to the mouth of the wadi, darkness had fallen completely, and every gully looked exactly like the last. His phone showed no signal, and its battery was dwindling fast. Forcing himself to stay calm, he recalled his grandfather's words from their first night together: when lost, find the North Star, and remember that this wadi runs from north to south. Slowly, keeping the bright star over his right shoulder, he began to pick his way downhill. Barely half an hour later, two torch beams swept across the rocks, and he heard Majid shouting his name. His grandfather reached him first and held him tightly, and although he did not raise his voice, the disappointment in his eyes hurt far more than any scolding could have done.

The next morning, Faisal apologised sincerely, and the three of them walked to the camera together, this time in silence. Majid slotted the memory card into his laptop, and they huddled around the screen in the shade of a large rock. The first few images showed nothing but swaying grass, but then a shape emerged from the darkness, pale gold and covered in dark rosettes. It was a leopard, a lean female, gazing straight into the lens with eyes that glowed silver in the infrared light. Majid let out a long breath and murmured a quiet prayer of thanks, while Faisal could not tear his eyes away from the screen. Then he clicked to the next image, and all three of them gasped: trotting at her heels was a small, clumsy cub.

"Do you understand what this means?" Majid whispered, his voice trembling with excitement. "A breeding female in the wild means there may be a population we knew nothing about." Almost immediately, however, his expression became serious. He explained that poachers and illegal traders would pay enormous sums for such an animal, and that even a single careless post online could reveal the location. Faisal felt his cheeks burn, because he had already imagined sharing the photograph with his friends and watching the reactions pour in. He took out his phone, looked at it for a long moment, and then put it firmly back in his pocket. "Not a word," he promised, and this time he fully intended to keep his promise.

Over the following weeks, a small team of scientists arrived quietly, and Faisal found himself drawn into their work. He learned to record GPS coordinates, to measure tracks with a ruler, and to sort hundreds of images without losing concentration. What struck him most, however, was how often the experts turned to his grandfather for advice. Abu Saleh knew which springs held water in the hottest months, where the ibex sheltered from the wind, and which paths a hunting cat would favour. "Your grandfather has been reading this landscape for sixty years," one researcher told Faisal. "No satellite could have taught us what he knows." Faisal, who had once dismissed the old man's stories as nothing more than folklore, felt a deep and unexpected pride.

On his final evening, Faisal sat beside his grandfather on the roof, watching the last light fade from the cliffs. He confessed that he had come to the mountains expecting to be bored, and that he was now leaving with his entire future rearranged. He intended to study ecology at university, he said, so that one day he could protect places like this one himself. Abu Saleh chuckled softly and placed a weathered hand on his shoulder. "The mountains keep their secrets," he said, "but they share them with those who learn to listen." Somewhere far up the wadi, faint but unmistakable, came that same rasping call, and neither of them said anything at all, because nothing more needed to be said.

pages.text: For as long as Noura could remember, Ramadan in her family had smelled of her grandmother's harees. Every evening a vast pot of wheat and meat would sit on the stove in the old house in Riyadh, slowly turning into something so smooth and fragrant that even the most impatient cousin would fall silent after the first spoonful. This year, however, the kitchen was unusually quiet. Two weeks before the holy month began, Grandmother Umm Saad had suffered a stroke, and although the doctors assured the family that her mind was as sharp as ever, she could no longer speak, and her right hand rested weakly in her lap. Nobody said it aloud, but everyone was wondering the same thing: who would make the harees now? At seventeen, Noura had never cooked anything more ambitious than pasta, yet she found herself volunteering before she had fully thought it through.

Her mother suggested she look through the cupboard above the old fridge, where her grandmother had kept her most treasured things. Behind a row of dusty jars of saffron and cardamom, Noura discovered a battered tin box decorated with faded roses. Inside lay a small notebook, its cover soft with age and its corners curled like dried leaves. When she opened it, her heart sank, because there was not a single word on any page. Instead, the paper was crowded with tiny drawings: crescent moons, palm trees, spirals, circles containing dots, and wavy lines that looked like water or perhaps steam. Then she remembered something her father had once told her, almost in passing, that her grandmother had grown up in a village with no school for girls and had never learned to read or write.

"So she invented her own alphabet," Noura whispered, running her finger over a row of miniature wheat grains. Her younger brother Hamad, who had wandered in looking for something to eat, peered over her shoulder with obvious scepticism. "It looks like a treasure map drawn by a five-year-old," he said. "You can't seriously be planning to cook from that." Noura gave him a look that made him take a step back. "Grandma cooked from this for fifty years without a single mistake," she replied. "If she could create it, then surely I can work out what it means."

That evening, after iftar, she spread the notebook across the dining table and approached it as she would a difficult exam question, slowly and methodically. Some symbols seemed fairly straightforward to interpret: three grains of wheat, she reasoned, probably meant three cups, and a crescent moon beside a bowl of wavy lines almost certainly meant soaking the wheat overnight. A spiral, repeated many times down the margin, had to refer to the long, patient stirring she had watched her grandmother do so many times. Other symbols, though, left her completely baffled, particularly a small circle with what looked like a flame trapped inside it. Every so often she carried the notebook into her grandmother's room, pointed at a drawing and waited. A slow nod meant she was on the right track, while a gentle frown sent her back to the table to think again.

Her first attempt, made the following afternoon, was, to put it kindly, a far cry from the real thing. The harees was gluey rather than silky, and although it was perfectly edible, it tasted of almost nothing at all. Hamad politely finished his bowl, which Noura suspected was more an act of brotherly loyalty than genuine enjoyment. When she brought a small portion to her grandmother, the old woman tasted it, closed her eyes for a moment, and then shook her head with great tenderness. With her good hand, she tapped the notebook firmly, right on the mysterious circle with the flame inside it. Noura sighed; it seemed she was back to square one.

Over the next few days, the kitchen became a laboratory of trial and error. Noura phoned her aunts, who each remembered the dish slightly differently, and her mother recalled that there had always been a particular smell in the house on the afternoons the harees was cooking. Hamad, who had quietly abandoned his scepticism and now spent hours beside her, suggested that the circle might represent a dried black lime. They tried it, piercing the hard little fruit and dropping it into the pot, and the result was undeniably better, with a faint, pleasant sharpness. Even so, when their grandmother tasted it, she merely smiled and tapped the symbol again, as if to say, "Closer, but not quite." Noura was beginning to wonder whether some recipes simply could not be passed on without words.

The breakthrough came, as breakthroughs often do, when she had stopped searching for it. Late one night, unable to sleep, Noura went downstairs and caught the scent of her father's incense burner, where a single piece of charcoal was still glowing. Suddenly, a memory she had not known she possessed came flooding back: her grandmother placing a tiny metal bowl on top of the harees, dropping a red-hot coal into it, pouring a spoonful of ghee over it, and quickly closing the lid on a cloud of fragrant smoke. That was the flame inside the circle, not an ingredient at all, but a technique, the old method of smoking food that her grandmother had learned as a child. The next morning, Noura described the memory, and her grandmother's face lit up as she nodded again and again, gripping her granddaughter's hand.

There was no time to lose, because the whole family was due to gather for iftar on the twenty-seventh night of Ramadan. Noura soaked the wheat under the light of the crescent moon, exactly as the notebook instructed, and began cooking just after the noon prayer. Hamad was dispatched to the garage to find charcoal, and he returned covered in black dust but looking enormously pleased with himself. For hours, the two of them took turns stirring, their arms aching, while the kitchen filled with the warm, comforting smell of wheat and slow-cooked lamb. Half an hour before sunset, with cars already pulling up outside, Noura heated the coal until it glowed, set it in the little bowl, poured over the ghee and slammed the lid shut. Smoke curled out from beneath it, and for a moment the kitchen smelled exactly as it had throughout her childhood.

When the call to prayer marked the end of the fast, the family broke their fast with dates and water, prayed together, and then gathered around the long table. Noura carried in the pot herself, her hands trembling slightly, and served the first bowl to her grandmother, who had been brought to the head of the table. A hush fell over the room as everyone waited. Umm Saad lifted the spoon slowly with her left hand, tasted, and remained perfectly still for what felt like an eternity. Then her eyes filled with tears, and she nodded, once, firmly and unmistakably. Her eldest son, Noura's uncle, took a spoonful from his own bowl and said quietly, "I never thought I would taste this again."

Later that night, when the guests had gone home, her grandmother beckoned Noura over and gestured for the notebook and a pen. With great effort, holding the pen awkwardly in her left hand, she drew a small, shaky star at the bottom of the harees page and pointed directly at Noura. Hamad, who had grown rather good at reading her expressions, grinned and said, "I think that means it's yours now." In the weeks that followed, Noura began copying the entire notebook into a new one, writing each recipe carefully in words but keeping every one of her grandmother's symbols beside them. She wanted her own children, and theirs, to understand that this was not merely a collection of recipes but a language, invented by a girl who had been denied an education yet had refused to let her knowledge disappear. On the first page, beneath the title, she drew a single small star.

pages.text: Faisal had always assumed that his grandfather's repair shop in the old quarter of Jeddah held nothing but dust and broken radios. For three summers he had swept its cracked floor, tested wires and listened to Grandpa Saleh grumble about how nothing was built to last anymore. Then, one humid afternoon in August, he pulled a drawer out too far and it crashed to the ground, scattering screws, faded receipts and a single cassette tape across the tiles. The label, written in elegant, slanting Arabic, read simply: 'For the sea – 1979.' Curiosity got the better of him, so he slid the tape into an ancient player on the workbench and pressed play. What came out was the warm, trembling voice of an oud, playing a melody so haunting that the hairs on his arms stood on end.

The tune rose and fell like waves against the harbour wall, circling back on itself as though searching for something it had lost. Faisal, who had been practising the oud for six years, found himself holding his breath, waiting for the phrase to resolve. It never did. Just as the melody climbed towards what was clearly meant to be its final note, the music stopped dead, leaving nothing but the soft hiss of empty tape. He rewound it twice, convinced the recording must have been damaged, but each time it broke off at precisely the same moment. It was, he realised, not broken at all; it had simply never been finished.

That evening, over small cups of cardamom coffee, Faisal placed the cassette on the table in front of his grandfather. Grandpa Saleh, whose hearing had been fading for years, leaned closer, squinting at the handwriting, and his face changed in a way Faisal had never seen before. 'Where did you find this?' he asked quietly, turning the tape over in his weathered fingers. Faisal explained, then asked who had been playing. For a long moment the old man said nothing, and Faisal began to wonder whether he had stumbled onto something he ought to have left alone. 'His name was Hamza,' Grandpa finally replied. 'He was the finest musician I ever knew, and once upon a time, he was my closest friend.'

The story came out slowly, in pieces, the way old memories often do. In their twenties, Saleh and Hamza had spent their evenings by the sea, Hamza composing on his oud while Saleh, who could barely hold a tune, offered opinions nobody had asked for. They had planned to perform the piece together at a wedding celebration for Hamza's brother, but they had argued bitterly over how it should end. Hamza wanted a gentle, fading conclusion, like the tide going out; Saleh insisted it should soar, like a ship setting sail. 'We were both too proud to give in,' Grandpa admitted, staring into his coffee. 'Hamza moved to Yanbu for work soon afterwards, and we never spoke again. Forty-five years, Faisal, over a single note.'

Faisal couldn't get the story out of his head, and over the following week he made it his mission to find out what had become of Hamza. He trawled through online forums, scrolled through local news archives and eventually came across a digital collection of traditional Hijazi music run by a university in Riyadh. Buried among hundreds of recordings was a short interview with a retired fisherman and oud player named Hamza Al-Juhani, recorded in Yanbu only two years earlier. The voice was older and rougher, but the playing in the background was unmistakable. With his heart pounding, Faisal emailed the archive, and to his astonishment, a reply arrived the next morning from Hamza's grandson, Turki. 'My grandfather would very much like to meet you,' it said. 'He still talks about a friend called Saleh.'

The following Friday, Faisal and his father made the three-hour drive north along the coast, the Red Sea glittering to their left the entire way. Hamza lived in a modest whitewashed house near the harbour, and he greeted them at the door with a warmth that instantly put Faisal at ease. Yet when Faisal noticed the old man's hands, twisted and swollen, his excitement faltered. 'Arthritis,' Hamza explained, following his gaze with a rueful smile. 'I haven't been able to play properly for nearly five years. These days, I leave the music to younger fingers than mine.' Over dates and tea, Faisal played him the cassette, and as the familiar melody filled the room, Hamza closed his eyes and his lips moved silently along with every note.

When the recording cut off, Hamza began to hum, softly at first and then with growing confidence, carrying the tune forward into the gentle, falling ending he had defended all those years ago. Faisal listened carefully, then asked, rather nervously, whether he might hear what Grandpa Saleh had wanted instead. Hamza laughed, a deep, surprised laugh. 'You want both endings? Your grandfather would never have allowed that.' Then he grew thoughtful and fell silent for a while. 'Perhaps that was our mistake all along,' he said eventually. 'We each believed there could only be one right answer, when the song might have had room for us both.'

Back in Jeddah, Faisal threw himself into the task of finishing the piece, practising late into the night until his fingertips ached. It proved far harder than he had anticipated, since the two endings seemed to pull in completely opposite directions, and for days every attempt sounded clumsy and forced. He was on the verge of giving up when, sitting on the roof one evening, he heard the call to prayer drift across the city and noticed how it rose before gently settling into stillness. Suddenly the solution seemed obvious: the melody could first soar like Saleh's departing ship, then slowly fade like Hamza's retreating tide. By dawn he had worked it out, note by careful note. He wrote the new ending down and, on the top of the page, gave it a title: 'The Ship and the Tide.'

A month later, the annual heritage festival was held in the historic heart of Al-Balad, among the carved wooden balconies of the old coral-stone houses. Faisal had been invited to perform, and, with Turki's help, he had arranged for Hamza to be driven down from Yanbu without telling Grandpa Saleh. When the two old men caught sight of each other in the crowd, both of them froze, as though forty-five years had folded into a single second. Then Hamza stepped forward, and Grandpa Saleh, whose pride had once seemed unshakeable, opened his arms. Faisal watched them embrace from the stage, swallowing the lump in his throat. Never had he felt so nervous, nor so certain that he was exactly where he was meant to be.

He began to play, and the familiar melody rolled out across the square, rising and falling like the sea. As he approached the point where the tape had always gone silent, he glanced down and saw his grandfather resting a hand on the edge of the stage, so that he could feel the vibrations even if he could not quite hear every note. The music climbed, soared triumphantly, and then, little by little, drifted down into a soft and peaceful close. For a moment there was complete silence, and then the square erupted into applause. Later, Grandpa Saleh pressed the old cassette into Faisal's hand and told him to record the finished version over the empty hiss at the end. 'It took three of us and almost half a century,' Hamza chuckled beside him, 'but at last the song has found its way home.'
