pages.text: At the Academy for Gifted Youth in the coastal city of Al-Marsa, everyone's ability was measured, ranked and quietly gossiped about, and Faris al-Qahtani's had never ranked particularly highly. He could capture any sound he heard and replay it later with flawless accuracy, from a seagull's cry to the precise rumble of a delivery lorry three streets away. His classmates, who could summon gusts of wind or sprint across rooftops, tended to treat his gift as little more than a party trick. "Do the call-to-prayer clock again," someone would plead at lunch, and Faris would oblige, even though it felt like being asked to juggle while others were saving lives. His cousin Yusuf, by contrast, could lift a loaded truck above his head, and his picture already hung in the main corridor. Faris was genuinely proud of him, yet he could not shake the nagging suspicion that he himself would only ever be a footnote in someone else's story.

On assessment day, the instructors announced the placements one by one, and Faris held his breath as the field teams were filled without him. When his name was finally read out, it was attached to a department he had barely heard of: the Listening Room, under the supervision of Ustadh Hamdan. A few students sniggered, because the Listening Room was widely regarded as the place where careers went to gather dust. Hamdan had once been known as the Silent Falcon, a hero whose exploits had been the stuff of legend before Faris was even born. Nowadays, however, he was an elderly man with a cane, a neatly trimmed white beard and a reputation for drinking more cardamom tea than was strictly advisable. Faris walked to his first session with his hands in his pockets, determined to make the best of a bad job.

The Listening Room turned out to be a far cry from the dusty storeroom he had imagined. Its walls were lined with thousands of labelled recordings: the creak of the old harbour bridge, the hum of the tram cables, the clatter of the fish market at dawn. "A city speaks constantly, if you know how to listen," Hamdan said, pouring two glasses of tea with a steadiness that belied his age. "Most people only hear noise, but every structure has its own voice, and that voice changes when something is wrong." He explained that he had spent decades cataloguing these sounds because, in his experience, disasters rarely arrived without warning; they simply whispered before they shouted. Faris, who had expected to be bored senseless, found himself leaning forward in his chair.

Over the following weeks, Hamdan put him through an apprenticeship that was as demanding as any combat training. Faris learned to distinguish the healthy groan of steel expanding in the afternoon heat from the sharper, uneven note of metal under genuine strain. He spent hours on the harbour bridge, absorbing its every sigh and shudder until he could have recognised it blindfolded. Little by little, he began to realise that his ability was not merely about replaying sounds but about remembering them so precisely that even the slightest change would leap out at him. "You see?" Hamdan remarked one evening, with a rare smile. "What they call a party trick is, in the right hands, an early-warning system." For the first time in years, Faris walked home feeling that his gift might actually matter.

The trouble began on the final night of the Al-Marsa Heritage Festival, when the whole city seemed to be gathered along the waterfront. Families had spread out picnic rugs, children waved glowing lanterns, and the trams across the harbour bridge were packed to capacity. Then, with barely an hour's notice, a ferocious sandstorm swept in from the desert, swallowing the fireworks in a choking orange haze. The emergency services sprang into action, and the Academy's field teams, Yusuf among them, were dispatched to guide people to shelter. Within minutes, the storm had knocked out the radio towers, leaving rescuers stranded in a fog of static. Faris, who had been ordered to stay at the station and keep out of the way, was standing on the platform when he heard it.

Beneath the howl of the wind, the bridge was making a sound he had never heard before, a deep, juddering note that rose and fell like a laboured breath. Faris compared it instantly with the hundreds of recordings stored in his memory, and his stomach dropped. One of the main support cables, battered by the gale, was beginning to fail. He rushed to the commanding officer, Captain Nasser, and blurted out his warning, but the captain barely glanced up from his useless radio. "Son, I've got a storm, a festival and no communications," he snapped. "I haven't got time for hunches." Faris stood there for a moment, torn between doing as he was told and doing what he knew to be right.

It was then that an idea struck him, so simple that he almost dismissed it. Every tram driver in Al-Marsa was trained to respond to a particular emergency tone, a sharp three-note signal that meant "stop immediately", and Faris had recorded it months ago purely out of curiosity. The radios might have been down, but the station's public-address speakers, wired directly into the trackside system, were still working. Faris grabbed the microphone, closed his eyes and replayed the signal with perfect precision, again and again, until it echoed down the entire length of the line. Through the swirling sand, he watched the headlights of the approaching trams shudder to a halt, one after another, just short of the bridge. Seconds later, with a screech that he would never forget, a section of the walkway ahead tore loose and plunged into the dark water below.

Not every tram had stopped in time, however; the first had already been halfway across and was now tilting precariously over the gap. Yusuf reached it within moments and braced the carriage on his shoulders, but the sand was so thick that the rescue team could not see which passengers were trapped. Faris sprinted onto the bridge, ignoring the shouts behind him, and focused all his attention on the chaos of sound. Among the wind and the groaning metal, he picked out a faint knocking on the far side, a man's laboured cough and, most distinctly, a little girl humming a nursery rhyme to keep herself calm. Calling out each position, he replayed the sounds back to the rescuers so they could follow them like a trail of breadcrumbs. One by one, all twenty-three passengers were carried to safety, and only then did Yusuf lower the carriage with a groan of relief.

By dawn, the storm had blown itself out, leaving the city coated in fine golden dust and astonishingly quiet. Captain Nasser found Faris sitting on the station steps, his ears still ringing, and to everyone's surprise, he offered him a hand. "I owe you an apology," he said gruffly. "Had I listened to you, I'd have closed that bridge an hour earlier." Yusuf collapsed beside his cousin and clapped him on the back so hard that Faris nearly toppled over. "I held up a tram," he laughed, "but you knew exactly where everyone was. I'd say you stole the show." The little girl who had been humming, now safely wrapped in a blanket beside her grandmother, waved at Faris shyly, and he found that he could not stop smiling.

When Faris finally returned to the Listening Room, Hamdan was waiting with two glasses of tea and an expression that was trying very hard not to look proud. "I was mocked for my ability too, you know," the old man admitted. "It took me years to understand that being quiet is not the same as being small." He then handed Faris a blank label and a pen, explaining that every new recording in the archive needed a name. Faris thought for a long moment before closing his eyes and replaying the sound he wanted to keep forever: the cheering of hundreds of grateful families on the waterfront at sunrise. Underneath it, in careful handwriting, he wrote: "Al-Marsa, the morning after." Then, beneath that, in smaller letters, he added the title Hamdan had insisted the city would soon be calling him: The Echo Keeper.

pages.text: By the time the family's car left the asphalt and began crawling across the Hisma desert, Rakan had already decided that the weekend would be uneventful. At seventeen, he considered himself something of an expert on camping, having watched more survival videos than anyone else in his class. His twelve-year-old sister, Lulwa, was pressed against the window, naming every rock formation after an animal. Their father drove in contented silence, while in the passenger seat their grandfather, whom everyone simply called Jaddi, studied the horizon as though he were reading a letter. Towering sandstone cliffs glowed orange in the late afternoon light, and the sand beneath them was as fine and pale as flour. "Paradise," Rakan murmured, and for once nobody argued with him.

They chose a spot on the flat, sandy floor of a broad wadi, sheltered on both sides by walls of rock that would block the wind. Rakan took charge of the tents with an air of quiet authority, hammering in pegs and tightening guy ropes until the canvas was stretched as taut as a drum. It took him the better part of an hour, and when he finally stepped back, sweat running down his forehead, he felt thoroughly pleased with himself. Lulwa arranged the cushions inside the family tent, while their father lit the charcoal for tea and grilled chicken. Jaddi, meanwhile, had wandered a little way off and was crouching beside a line of dry twigs and debris tangled at the base of a boulder. He picked up a bleached stick, turned it over in his fingers, and said nothing at all.

Just as the sun dipped behind the cliffs, Jaddi pointed towards the mountains far to the north. Above them hung a bank of dark, bruised cloud, and every few seconds it flickered silently from within. "There is rain over there," he said calmly, "and this wadi is the road it will take." Rakan glanced up at the sky directly overhead, which was perfectly clear and already scattered with the first stars. "Jaddi, that storm must be fifty kilometres away," he protested, trying not to sound impatient. His grandfather tapped the stick he was still holding. "Then explain to me how this branch came to be sitting here, in the middle of the desert, wedged so neatly against that rock."

Their father exchanged a look with Jaddi and, without further discussion, announced that they were moving camp. Rakan could hardly believe his ears; all that careful work was about to be undone because of a cloud on the other side of the world. Still, he had been brought up to respect his elders, so he swallowed his objections and began pulling up the pegs he had driven in so proudly. They carried everything up a steep, rocky slope to a wide ledge some ten metres above the wadi floor. The ground there was hard and uneven, and the new tent sagged a little no matter how hard Rakan tugged at it. "It looks like a collapsed cake," Lulwa giggled, and he shot her a glare that would have curdled milk.

From their ledge they could see the headlights of three four-wheel drives pulling into the wadi further down, followed by the cheerful thump of music. A group of young men, perhaps university students from Riyadh, began setting up camp right in the middle of the dry riverbed. "Come with me," their father said to Rakan, picking up a torch, "it would be wrong to say nothing." The two of them picked their way down and greeted the group, who were friendly and immediately offered them coffee and dates. When their father explained, politely, that flood water might come down the valley during the night, one of the young men grinned. "With respect, uncle, it hasn't rained here in months," he said, and his friends laughed good-naturedly as they returned to their fire.

Back on the ledge, Rakan sat beside his grandfather, wrapped in a thick blanket, and admitted that he felt a little foolish. "They looked at us as if we were mad," he said, "and to be honest, I'm not sure they were wrong." Jaddi poured him a small cup of cardamom coffee and smiled in the darkness. "When I was your age, my own father made me sleep on a hill every night we travelled, and I resented him for it," he said. "Then one spring I saw a whole herd of camels swept away in a valley where not a single drop had fallen." He fell silent, and Rakan found himself staring at the distant flickering clouds with entirely new eyes. Somewhere far below, the music played on.

Rakan was woken a little after two in the morning by a sound he had never heard before, a deep, rushing growl like an enormous train approaching through the rock. He scrambled out of the tent just as his father's torch beam swept across the wadi below. What had been a carpet of silky sand only hours earlier was now a churning brown torrent, carrying branches, stones and foam at frightening speed. Further down, headlights were swinging wildly as the young men shouted to one another, desperately trying to start their engines. One car had already been caught, its front wheels sinking as the water surged around its doors. "Grab the rope from the boot!" his father yelled, and Rakan was already running.

They raced along the ledge until they were directly above the stranded group, who had clambered onto the roof of the trapped vehicle. Rakan's hands were shaking, but he managed to tie the rope securely around a jutting boulder, exactly as he had seen in so many videos. His father lowered the other end, and one by one the young men hauled themselves up the slope, soaked to the skin and gasping for breath. Lulwa held the torch steady the whole time, her face pale but determined, while Jaddi called out instructions about where to place their feet. When the last of them reached the top, nobody spoke for a long moment. Below them, the abandoned car groaned, tilted, and was dragged slowly out of sight.

Dawn revealed a landscape that seemed to have been redrawn overnight. The flood had subsided as suddenly as it had arrived, leaving behind a glistening layer of mud, flattened bushes and, in the exact spot where Rakan had first pitched the family's tent, a deep channel gouged into the earth. The young men, wrapped in spare blankets, sat around the fire sipping tea, still visibly shaken. Their leader, the one who had laughed the night before, approached Jaddi and kissed his forehead in the traditional gesture of respect. "Forgive us, uncle," he said quietly, "we owe you far more than an apology." Jaddi simply patted his shoulder and told him that the desert was a generous teacher, provided one was willing to listen.

That afternoon, as their father arranged for a tow truck to recover what remained of the lost car, Rakan wandered down to inspect the new channel. He crouched beside it and noticed fresh branches lodged against the rocks, exactly like the old one that had caught his grandfather's eye. It dawned on him that the clues had been there all along, written plainly in the sand for anyone who knew how to read them. That evening he took out a small notebook and, beneath the date, wrote a single sentence: "Never trust a clear sky over a dry river." Lulwa peered over his shoulder and declared that their sagging tent had been the most beautiful tent in the whole of Arabia. For once, Rakan could not have agreed with her more.

So, are we agreed that the library would be the most useful option?

In the long run, online learning is likely to become even more widespread.

words.ex: Her case was so watertight that nobody on the opposing team could find a weakness in it.
The crux of the problem is that exams reward memory rather than understanding.
If you make a bold claim, you need to substantiate it with reliable data.
Critics argue that rote learning leaves students unable to apply what they know.
A research project allows students to carry out an in-depth study of a topic they care about.
She presented a compelling argument backed by several international studies.

dialogue.t: So, should secondary schools replace some exams with long-term research projects? What's your position?
I believe they should. The crux of my argument is that exams measure how well you perform on one day, not what you've genuinely learnt.
That's a big claim. Can you back it up?
Certainly. This is borne out by the fact that many students forget most exam content within weeks, whereas skills developed through projects tend to last.
And what do projects offer beyond better memory?
Not only does a project develop research skills, but it also teaches time management and independence, which universities value highly.
So what's your conclusion?
It follows, therefore, that a balanced system with fewer exams and more projects would prepare students far better for real life.

grammar.title: Inversion after 'Not only'
grammar.ar: عندما نبدأ الجملة بـ Not only للتأكيد، نقلب ترتيب الفاعل والفعل المساعد كما في السؤال: Not only does it... وليس Not only it does. إذا لم يكن في الجملة فعل مساعد نستخدم do/does/did. يأتي الجزء الثاني عادةً مع but ... also. هذا الأسلوب رسمي ويُضفي قوة على الحجة في النقاش والكتابة الأكاديمية.
examples: Not only does project work build confidence, but it also encourages creativity.
Not only did the study involve thousands of students, but it was also repeated in three countries.
Not only are exams stressful, but they also fail to reflect long-term ability.

words.ex: I'm willing to concede that some influencers do valuable charity work.
Teenagers often see successful athletes as role models.
Followers tend to trust influencers who seem authentic rather than overly polished.

words.ar: يروّج لـ / يُصادق على (منتج أو فكرة)
words.ex: Many influencers are paid to endorse products they have never actually used.
Some content focuses on superficial things like appearance and expensive brands.
Even after hearing the counterarguments, she stood her ground.

dialogue.t: Influencers inspire millions of young people. Surely that makes them positive role models?
Granted, some of them promote healthy habits and education; that said, many others glorify wealth and appearance.
But a lot of influencers are open about their struggles, like anxiety. That's authentic and helpful.
While there is some truth in the idea that openness reduces stigma, it overlooks the fact that much of that content is still sponsored.
Young people aren't naive, though. They know when something is an advert.
I'd go along with that up to a point, but research shows younger teenagers often can't distinguish ads from genuine opinions.
So you think they're mostly a negative influence?
Admittedly, a few are excellent role models, yet the overall picture is one of superficial values being sold to impressionable audiences.

grammar.title: Concessive structures
grammar.ar: تُستخدم تراكيب التنازل للاعتراف بنقطة صحيحة لدى الطرف الآخر ثم العودة إلى موقفك. نضع العبارة الاعترافية أولاً مثل Granted أو Admittedly أو While، ثم نتبعها بأداة تُعيد الموقف مثل that said أو yet أو but. بعد While نستخدم جملة كاملة، وبعد Granted/Admittedly نضع فاصلة ثم الجملة. هذا الأسلوب يجعلك تبدو منصفاً ومقنعاً في الوقت نفسه.
examples: Granted, influencers can raise awareness; that said, their motives are often commercial.
While it is true that some content is educational, most of it is designed purely for entertainment.
Admittedly, I follow a few influencers myself, yet I rarely trust their recommendations.

words.ex: Your argument is based on the assumption that all students misuse their phones.
The study was flawed because it only surveyed one school.
She calmly rebutted each of her opponent's points.
Saying that all teenagers are addicted to phones is a sweeping generalisation.
A total ban might be counterproductive if students simply hide their phones.
It's important to be tactful when you point out a flaw in someone's reasoning.

dialogue.t: Smartphones should be banned in classrooms. They're a constant distraction, so students can't possibly learn with them around.
That argument rests on the assumption that phones are only ever used for entertainment, which isn't always the case.
Well, if students have phones, they'll obviously check social media.
I'm not sure that necessarily follows, because many students use them responsibly for dictionaries, calculators and research.
Even so, removing all technology is the safest option.
If we take that to its logical conclusion, we'd have to ban laptops and tablets too, which would be clearly counterproductive.
But studies show test scores rise when phones are banned.
With respect, the evidence suggests otherwise: several recent studies found no significant change when phones were used with clear rules.

grammar.title: Noun + that-clause for abstract ideas
grammar.ar: في النقاش الرسمي نستخدم أسماء مجردة مثل assumption وevidence وidea وfact وclaim تتبعها جملة تبدأ بـ that لشرح محتوى الفكرة. هذه الجملة ليست جملة وصلية بل تشرح مضمون الاسم نفسه، لذلك لا يمكن استبدال that بـ which. هذا التركيب يساعدك على تحديد الفكرة التي تنتقدها بدقة قبل الرد عليها.
examples: Your point rests on the assumption that teachers cannot manage technology.
There is little evidence that banning phones improves concentration.
I disagree with the claim that students lack self-control.

words.ex: Good speakers hedge their predictions instead of presenting them as facts.
It's plausible that AI tutors will become common in the next decade.
Few experts believe that AI will completely supplant human teachers.
Adaptive software adjusts the difficulty of exercises to each learner's level.
The pandemic caused an unprecedented shift to online learning.
The idea that schools will disappear entirely seems rather far-fetched.

dialogue.t: Do you think AI tutors will replace teachers in the future?
It would seem that AI is improving rapidly, but replacing teachers completely sounds far-fetched to me.
What about remote learning? Will it become the norm?
There's every likelihood that hybrid models will grow, especially at university level.
So you're confident schools will move mostly online?
Not exactly. It's by no means certain that younger students can stay motivated without face-to-face contact.
And AI tutors specifically?
Adaptive AI tools are bound to become more widespread, although teachers may well remain essential for motivation. To all intents and purposes, AI will be an assistant rather than a replacement.

grammar.title: Expressing degrees of certainty
grammar.ar: في الإنجليزية الأكاديمية نتجنّب الجزم المطلق ونعبّر عن درجة الثقة بدقة. للتأكيد القوي نستخدم is bound to أو There's every likelihood that، وللاحتمال المتوسط may well أو It would seem that، وللشك It's by no means certain that. اختيار التعبير المناسب يُظهر تفكيراً نقدياً ودقة، وهو مطلوب في اختبارات مثل IELTS وCambridge C1.
examples: Online courses are bound to become cheaper as technology improves.
AI tutors may well transform how students revise for exams.
It's by no means certain that every family will have reliable internet access.

words.ex: Doctors sometimes face a difficult ethical dilemma when resources are limited.
Is animal testing ever justifiable if it saves human lives?

words.ar: منحدر زلق (خطوة تقود إلى عواقب أسوأ)
words.ex: Some people fear that genetic screening is a slippery slope towards designer babies.
Wealth inequality has widened in many countries over the last few decades.
Animals cannot give consent, which makes testing on them morally complex.
Even well-meant laws can have unintended consequences.

dialogue.t: Let's consider genetic screening of embryos. Can it be justified?
On the one hand, screening could be justified on the grounds that it prevents serious inherited diseases.
But some parents might want to choose eye colour or intelligence.
Exactly. Where do we draw the line between preventing illness and designing a child? That's the real slippery slope.
What makes it so difficult, in your view?
The moral dimension here is that we're making decisions for people who can't give consent, and we may reinforce inequality if only the rich can afford it.
So should it be banned?
Not entirely. Were we to ban it completely, the consequences might be more suffering from preventable diseases, so strict regulation seems wiser.

grammar.title: Inverted conditionals with 'Were'
grammar.ar: في الأسلوب الرسمي يمكن حذف if من الجملة الشرطية الثانية ووضع were في بداية الجملة: Were we to ban it بدلاً من If we were to ban it. يُستخدم هذا التركيب للحديث عن مواقف افتراضية أو مستبعدة بطريقة رسمية وأنيقة. بعد were نضع الفاعل ثم to + الفعل المجرد، والجملة الرئيسية تحتوي عادةً على would أو might أو could.
examples: Were governments to tax the wealthy more heavily, public services might improve.
Were scientists to stop animal testing overnight, some medical research could stall.
Were we to allow unlimited genetic selection, society might become even more divided.

words.ex: The motion for today's debate is that university should be free for everyone.
The proposition argued that free education is a basic right.
Who should bear the cost, students or the taxpayer?
Free tuition would make higher education accessible to students from poorer families.
Education is one of the most powerful drivers of social mobility.
Critics say that funding every degree is financially unsustainable.

dialogue.t: The floor is yours. Please give your opening statement.
Thank you. I stand firmly in favour of the motion because free university is the most effective way to boost social mobility.
Free university places a huge burden on the taxpayer, many of whom never benefit from it.
My opponent has claimed that taxpayers gain nothing, but graduates earn more, pay more tax and contribute to a stronger economy for everyone.
Yet in countries with free tuition, universities are often overcrowded and underfunded.
Let me draw your attention to Germany and Finland, where free tuition coexists with world-class universities.
Time for your closing statement.
In light of everything we've heard, it is clear that free university is not a luxury but an investment. I urge you to support the motion.

grammar.title: Reporting an opponent's claims
grammar.ar: عند الرد على الخصم نستخدم أفعال النقل مثل claim وargue وsuggest وmaintain وinsist، وغالباً بزمن المضارع التام: My opponent has claimed that... لأن الكلام قيل للتو وما زال مهماً الآن. اختيار الفعل يكشف موقفك: claim يوحي بالشك، بينما point out يوحي بالموافقة. بعد هذه الأفعال نضع that ثم جملة كاملة، ثم نتبعها بـ but لتقديم الرد.
examples: My opponent has argued that free tuition lowers standards, but the evidence does not support this.
The opposition has suggested that loans encourage responsibility, yet they also deter poorer students.
It has been claimed that graduates should pay for their own degrees, but society as a whole benefits from them.

words.ex: Al-Ula's ancient sites are a vital part of the Kingdom's heritage, and they're now attracting visitors from all over the world.
The pace of modernisation in Riyadh has been so rapid that some neighbourhoods are almost unrecognisable compared to ten years ago.
Many young Saudis feel that speaking their local dialect is an important part of their cultural identity.
The generation gap becomes obvious when my grandfather and I talk about careers. He values stability, while I value flexibility.
Young people tend to embrace change more readily, partly because they've grown up surrounded by it.
Some people worry that globalisation could gradually erode traditional values if we're not careful.

dialogue.t: Have you noticed how much Jeddah has changed recently? The whole city has undergone a profound transformation in just a few years.
Absolutely. But my grandmother often says she misses the old souqs and the way neighbours used to know each other.
I get that. Whereas my grandparents' generation grew up in tight-knit communities, young people today are connected to the whole world but sometimes don't know who lives next door.
Exactly. It would be a shame if those strong community ties were lost just because life has become faster.
Still, I think Vision 2030 is trying to protect heritage too. Look at the restoration of Al-Balad and Diriyah.
True. There's a delicate balance to be struck between attracting global investment and preserving what makes us unique.
And I suppose our generation will be the ones deciding where that balance lies.
That's quite a responsibility, but I'm optimistic. Tradition and progress don't have to be enemies.

grammar.title: Present Perfect for Long-Term Change
grammar.ar: نستخدم المضارع التام (has/have + التصريف الثالث) للحديث عن تغيّرات بدأت في الماضي وما زالت نتائجها واضحة في الحاضر، مثل: has undergone, has evolved, has transformed. ويمكن تقويته بظروف مثل dramatically أو profoundly أو over the past decade. أما إذا ذكرنا وقتاً محدداً منتهياً في الماضي مثل in 2016 فنستخدم الماضي البسيط بدلاً منه.
examples: Saudi society has undergone a profound transformation over the past decade.
The role of women in the workforce has changed dramatically since the reforms began.
Entertainment options have expanded enormously, whereas they were very limited when my parents were young.

words.ex: Some teachers claim that students' attention spans have shrunk since short-form videos became popular.
Relying on GPS for every journey may weaken certain cognitive skills, such as spatial memory.
Over-reliance on AI tools for homework could prevent students from developing their own writing style.
Group projects done face to face tend to foster deeper friendships than online chats.

words.ar: التوقف المؤقت عن استخدام الأجهزة الرقمية
words.ex: After a week-long digital detox in the desert, I felt far more relaxed and creative.
Constant connectivity means we're never truly off duty, even during family gatherings.

dialogue.t: Do you think AI is making us smarter or lazier?
Honestly, I think it's a bit of both. There's a growing body of evidence to suggest that heavy smartphone use reduces our ability to focus for long periods.
I've definitely noticed that with myself. The more we rely on our phones to remember things, the less we bother memorising anything.
And paradoxically, social media has made us more isolated, even though it's supposed to connect us.
That's true, but what about creativity? My cousin uses AI to brainstorm design ideas, and her work has improved a lot.
Maybe, but it's debatable whether AI genuinely makes people more creative or just more productive.
Fair point. I suppose it depends on whether you use it as a starting point or as a replacement for thinking.
Exactly. The tool itself isn't the problem. It's how we choose to use it.

grammar.title: The more ..., the less ... (Double Comparatives)
grammar.ar: تُستخدم هذه البنية للتعبير عن علاقة تناسبية بين أمرين، أي أن تغيّر أحدهما يؤدي إلى تغيّر الآخر. تتكوّن من the + صيغة المقارنة + فاعل + فعل، ثم فاصلة، ثم the + صيغة المقارنة + فاعل + فعل. ويمكن استخدام more أو less أو صفة مقارنة مثل harder أو easier.
examples: The more we rely on AI, the less we trust our own judgement.
The longer I spend scrolling, the harder it becomes to concentrate on my studies.
The more connected we are online, the lonelier some people seem to feel.

words.ex: Choosing public transport over driving is one simple way to reduce your carbon footprint.
There needs to be greater accountability for companies that pollute rivers and oceans.
Saudi Arabia is investing heavily in renewable energy, particularly solar power, given its abundant sunshine.
Governments could incentivise people to buy electric cars by offering tax reductions.

words.ar: التضليل البيئي (ادّعاء الشركات الاهتمام بالبيئة كذباً)
words.ex: Labelling a plastic bottle as eco-friendly just because it's green is a classic example of greenwashing.
Planting millions of trees under the Saudi Green Initiative could deliver tangible benefits for air quality.

dialogue.t: Who do you think should take the lead on climate change: governments, companies or ordinary people?
In my view, the onus is on governments to set strict regulations. Individuals can only do so much.
I partly agree, but corporations produce a huge share of emissions. Unless decisive action is taken against major polluters, nothing will really change.
Sure, but people still have a role. If nobody buys products from irresponsible brands, companies will be forced to adapt.
It's all very well saying consumers should boycott those brands, but in practice, sustainable options are often more expensive.
That's a fair point. A more pragmatic approach would be to make green products cheaper through subsidies.
Exactly. So it's really a shared responsibility, with governments creating the conditions for everyone else to act.
I think we've reached a compromise, then. Nobody gets to blame someone else entirely.

grammar.title: Conditions with 'Unless'
grammar.ar: تعني unless «إلّا إذا» أو «ما لم»، وهي تعادل if ... not. نستخدمها للتحذير أو لوضع شرط ضروري لحدوث أمر ما. يأتي بعدها فعل مثبت وليس منفياً، فنقول unless we act ولا نقول unless we don't act. ويكون الفعل بعدها غالباً في المضارع حتى عند الحديث عن المستقبل.
examples: Unless decisive action is taken, global temperatures will continue to rise.
Companies won't change their practices unless they face serious financial penalties.
Unless renewable energy becomes affordable, many families will keep using fossil fuels.

words.ex: The discovery of oil in 1938 was a major turning point in the history of the Arabian Peninsula.
The development of vaccines was a medical breakthrough that saved millions of lives.
Historians still debate how events would have unfolded if the war had ended a year earlier.

words.ar: عند النظر إلى الوراء / بعد معرفة النتائج
words.ex: In hindsight, the decision to invest in education was one of the smartest moves the country ever made.
A single invention can alter the course of human history.
Some argue that the invention of the internet was inevitable, even if it had happened a few decades later.

dialogue.t: I've been reading about Ibn al-Haytham. Had he not developed his ideas about optics, modern cameras would probably look very different.
That's fascinating. He must have faced a lot of scepticism at the time, experimenting in ways nobody else did.
Definitely. And think about penicillin. If it hadn't been for Fleming's accidental discovery, we might still be dying from simple infections.
True, although it's conceivable that someone else might have discovered it a few years later anyway.
Maybe, but those few years could have cost millions of lives.
Good point. What about the discovery of oil here? Had it not been found, Saudi Arabia would probably have developed in a completely different way.
Probably through trade and pilgrimage alone. In hindsight, it really did alter the course of the whole region.
It makes you wonder which events happening today will seem like turning points in a hundred years.

grammar.title: Inverted Third Conditional (Had + subject + past participle)
grammar.ar: في الأسلوب الرسمي أو الأكاديمي يمكن حذف if من الشرط الثالث وتقديم had على الفاعل، فتصبح If he had not discovered ... هي Had he not discovered .... يُستخدم هذا الشرط للحديث عن أحداث ماضية لم تحدث وتخيّل نتائجها المختلفة. لاحظ أن not تأتي بعد الفاعل وليس بعد had مباشرة، ولا نستخدم الاختصار hadn't في هذه البنية.
examples: Had the printing press not been invented, knowledge would have spread far more slowly.
Had scientists ignored Fleming's findings, penicillin might not have been developed until much later.
Had oil not been discovered in 1938, the Saudi economy would probably look very different today.

words.ar: مهارات قابلة للنقل (تفيد في أكثر من مجال)
words.ex: Communication and problem-solving are transferable skills that are useful in almost any profession.
In a fast-changing job market, adaptability may be more valuable than any single qualification.
Many jobs that existed twenty years ago, such as video rental clerks, are now completely obsolete.
Automation is likely to replace many repetitive tasks in factories and offices.
Lifelong learning is essential if you want to stay relevant throughout your career.
Impressive credentials might get you an interview, but your personality is what gets you the job.

dialogue.t: My parents keep telling me a university degree is the only path to a good job. Do you agree?
Not entirely. A degree still matters, but it's no longer enough to just have a certificate on the wall.
Right. From what I've read, employers are increasingly placing emphasis on soft skills like teamwork and creativity.
Exactly. What really gives someone the edge is practical experience, such as internships or personal projects.
And with AI developing so fast, some careers won't even exist in ten years.
That's true. I'm inclined to think that routine data-entry jobs will become obsolete, whereas jobs involving empathy, like nursing or counselling, will always be needed.
So maybe the smartest strategy is to get a degree but never stop learning new skills.
Definitely. Lifelong learning is the real key to success now.

grammar.title: Cleft Sentences with 'What'
grammar.ar: الجملة المشقوقة بـ What أسلوب يُستخدم لتسليط الضوء على معلومة مهمة وجذب انتباه المستمع إليها. تتكوّن من What + جملة + is/was + الجزء المراد التأكيد عليه. فبدلاً من قول Experience gives you the edge نقول What gives you the edge is experience. وهذا الأسلوب شائع في المحادثة والنقاش عند التأكيد على رأي.
examples: What really gives someone the edge is the ability to learn quickly.
What employers want these days is people who can think critically.
What worries me most is that some degrees may not prepare students for real jobs.

words.ex: During health crises, misinformation can spread faster than accurate medical advice.
Before sharing a news story, check whether it comes from a credible source.

words.ar: يأخذ الأمر على ظاهره دون تحقّق
words.ex: You shouldn't take every viral video at face value, since many are edited or staged.
A fake quote attributed to a famous footballer went viral within hours.

words.ar: التحيّز التأكيدي (تصديق ما يوافق آراءنا المسبقة)
words.ex: Confirmation bias makes us more likely to believe stories that match what we already think.
Journalists are expected to verify facts with at least two independent sources.

dialogue.t: Did you see that post claiming a famous restaurant chain was closing all its branches in Saudi Arabia?
Yes, and it turned out to be completely false! What concerns me most is the extent to which people share things without checking.
I know. My uncle forwards everything on WhatsApp. Before taking a message at face value, one should at least look for an official source.
The problem is that fake stories are often designed to be emotional and shocking.
Exactly. It's easy to be swayed by dramatic headlines, which is precisely why schools should teach media literacy.
And with AI-generated images now, the line between real and fake content has become increasingly blurred.
That's scary. I've started using reverse image searches to check suspicious photos.
That's a great habit. If more young people did that, misinformation wouldn't spread so easily.

grammar.title: Sentential Relative Clauses with 'which'
grammar.ar: تُستخدم which بعد فاصلة لتعليق على الجملة السابقة كلّها وليس على كلمة واحدة فقط. وتعادل في العربية قولنا «وهذا ما...» أو «الأمر الذي...». تأتي دائماً بعد فاصلة، ولا يجوز استبدالها بـ that أو what في هذه الحالة. وهي مفيدة جداً لربط الأفكار وإبداء الرأي أو ذكر النتائج.
examples: It's easy to be swayed by emotional headlines, which is precisely why we need to think critically.
Many people never check the original source, which allows fake news to spread rapidly.
AI can now create realistic fake videos, which makes verifying information more difficult than ever.

words.ex: Examiners expect you to elaborate on your answers rather than just saying yes or no.
I've always been drawn to subjects that involve solving real-world problems.
I grew up in a bustling neighbourhood where the markets stay open until midnight.
After a long day of revision, I usually unwind by going for a walk along the corniche.
To some extent, my choice of subjects was influenced by my older brother.
I'm hoping to pursue a career in architecture once I finish school.

dialogue.t: Let's talk about your studies. Do you enjoy the subjects you're taking at the moment?
To be honest, I'd say I enjoy most of them, mainly because they're quite practical. Chemistry in particular has really grown on me this year.
And what about your hometown? Is it a good place for young people?
It depends to some extent on what you're into. If you like a bustling atmosphere, it's fantastic, but there aren't many quiet green spaces where you can unwind.
What kinds of hobbies do you have?
I've always been drawn to photography ever since my uncle lent me his old camera when I was about twelve. I've been taking photos of street life ever since.
Has the way you spend your free time changed recently?
Definitely. These days I find myself reading more than I used to, probably because I'm trying to cut down on screen time before exams.

grammar.title: Present Perfect with 'ever since' and 'find myself + -ing'
grammar.ar: نستخدم المضارع التام (have/has + التصريف الثالث) مع ever since للحديث عن شيء بدأ في الماضي وما زال مستمراً حتى الآن، ويأتي بعد ever since فعلٌ في الماضي البسيط يحدد نقطة البداية. يخطئ كثير من المتحدثين بالعربية فيقولون I am interested since... والصحيح I have been interested since... لأن العربية لا تميّز هذا الزمن. أما تعبير find myself + فعل بـ ing فيعبّر عن عادة جديدة لاحظتها في نفسك، ويجعل إجابتك تبدو طبيعية وعفوية في الجزء الأول من الامتحان.
examples: I've loved football ever since I watched my first World Cup match.
She has lived in Amman ever since her family moved there in 2015.
These days I find myself listening to podcasts instead of music.

words.ex: Overcoming that setback made me far more determined to succeed.
Failing my first driving test was a turning point in how I prepare for challenges.
Even when I wanted to give up, my coach encouraged me to persevere.

words.ar: المرونة والقدرة على التعافي من الصعوبات
words.ex: My grandmother's resilience during hard times has always inspired me.

words.ar: بعد فوات الأوان / عند النظر إلى الماضي
words.ex: In hindsight, I should have asked for help much earlier.
I still have a vivid memory of standing on stage, my hands shaking.

dialogue.t: I'd like you to describe a challenge you overcame. You have one minute to prepare, and then please speak for up to two minutes.
I'd like to talk about a public speaking competition, which took place at my school about two years ago. I'd never spoken in front of more than ten people before.
I'd been practising for weeks, but on the day my mind went completely blank for the first few seconds. I can still picture the hall, which was packed with parents and teachers.
What made it particularly memorable was that I managed to recover. I took a deep breath, looked at my notes, and carried on as if nothing had happened.
Looking back, I realise that the setback actually helped me, because it forced me to stay calm under pressure. It taught me the value of preparation, but also of resilience.
Thank you. Do you still enjoy speaking in public?
Surprisingly, yes. In hindsight, that competition was a real turning point for my confidence.

grammar.title: Narrative tenses for storytelling
grammar.ar: لسرد قصة مشوّقة في الجزء الثاني من IELTS نمزج بين عدة أزمنة: الماضي البسيط للأحداث الرئيسية المتتابعة، والماضي المستمر لوصف الخلفية والمشهد، والماضي التام (had + التصريف الثالث) لحدث وقع قبل حدث آخر في الماضي. يميل المتحدثون بالعربية إلى استخدام الماضي البسيط فقط، لكن التنويع في الأزمنة يرفع درجتك في معيار القواعد ويجعل القصة أوضح وأكثر حيوية.
examples: I had never travelled alone before, so I was extremely nervous.
While I was waiting for the results, my phone suddenly rang.
By the time we reached the summit, the sun had already set.

words.ex: Both photographs depict people working under considerable pressure.
The student in the second picture looks rather apprehensive about the exam.
The climbers must feel exhilarated after reaching the top.
In this part of the test, you need to speculate about why the people are there.
Her facial expression conveys a sense of relief.
The nurse appears to be under a lot of strain during the night shift.

dialogue.t: Here are your pictures. They show people dealing with difficult moments. Compare two of them and say how the people might be feeling.
Both pictures depict people facing some kind of challenge, but whereas the first shows a team working together, the second focuses on one individual on her own.
The person on the left looks as though he's just received some bad news. He's staring at his phone and he seems quite apprehensive.
In the second picture, the athlete could be about to start a race. I'd imagine she might be feeling a mixture of excitement and nerves because everyone's watching her.
Which person do you think is under more pressure?
It's hard to say for certain, but I'd probably go for the athlete. Her whole performance depends on a few seconds, whereas the man may have time to sort out his problem.
Thank you.

grammar.title: Modals of speculation and 'look as though'
grammar.ar: عند التخمين حول الصور نستخدم أفعالاً ناقصة تعبّر عن درجة اليقين: must للتأكد الكبير، وmight/may/could للاحتمال، وcan't للنفي المؤكد. وللتخمين حول الماضي نضيف have + التصريف الثالث مثل might have lost. كما نستخدم looks as though / looks as if متبوعة بجملة كاملة فيها فاعل وفعل، وليس اسماً فقط، فلا نقول looks as though tired بل looks as though he is tired.
examples: She must be exhausted after working all night.
They might have just finished an important meeting.
The boy looks as though he's trying not to laugh.

words.ex: Let's weigh up the pros and cons of each option before we decide.
You've made a compelling argument for choosing the library project.
It took us a while, but we eventually reached a consensus.
Building a new sports centre isn't really feasible on such a small budget.
I think schools should prioritise students' mental health.
That's a fair point, and I'll definitely take it on board.

dialogue.t: So, we need to discuss how these ideas could help young people manage stress. Shall we start with the idea of longer school breaks?
Sure. I think it's quite effective, but what's your take on the mentoring programme? Personally, I find it the most compelling option.
I can see the benefits, but I'm not sure it's feasible. Schools would need to train a lot of staff.
I see where you're coming from, but wouldn't you agree that talking to someone experienced has a longer-lasting impact than just having more free time?
That's a fair point, and I'll take it on board. Breaks only help in the short term, I suppose.
Exactly. And sports facilities are useful, but not everyone enjoys exercise, so I wouldn't prioritise them.
Right. So, are we agreed that mentoring would be the most beneficial option?
Yes, I think we've reached a consensus. Mentoring it is.

grammar.title: Negative questions to persuade and invite agreement
grammar.ar: نستخدم الأسئلة المنفية مثل wouldn't you agree...? وisn't it true that...? وdon't you think...? لا لطلب معلومة، بل لإقناع الشريك بلطف ودعوته للموافقة على رأينا. هذا الأسلوب يجعل النقاش تفاعلياً ومهذباً بدلاً من فرض الرأي مباشرة، وهو ما يكافئه الممتحنون في معيار التواصل التفاعلي. انتبه إلى أن الفعل المساعد المنفي يأتي قبل الفاعل: Don't you think وليس You don't think في هذا السياق.
examples: Wouldn't you agree that cost is the most important factor here?
Isn't it true that most students prefer practical activities?
Don't you think we should focus on the long-term benefits?

words.ex: Excessive social media use can be detrimental to teenagers' self-esteem.
Artificial intelligence is a double-edged sword for the job market.
Group projects foster teamwork and communication skills.
Expensive private tutoring may widen the gap between rich and poor students.
As technology advances, some traditional jobs will inevitably disappear.
Digital literacy should be taught alongside reading and maths.

dialogue.t: Do you think technology has improved the quality of education?
That's quite a complex issue; broadly speaking, I'd say it has, but it's something of a double-edged sword.
In what way?
One could argue that online resources give students access to world-class teaching, however, they can also be distracting and may even be detrimental to concentration.
And how do you think schools will change in the future?
In the long run, digital literacy is likely to become just as important as traditional subjects. Inevitably, teachers will act more as guides than as sources of information.
Are young people today better prepared for work than their parents were?
Compared with previous generations, we certainly have more technical skills, but I'm not convinced schools foster the soft skills, like negotiation, that employers really value.

grammar.title: Hedging and impersonal language
grammar.ar: في النقاشات المجرّدة (الجزء الثالث في IELTS والجزء الرابع في C1) نستخدم لغة التحفّظ لتبدو إجاباتنا تحليلية ومتوازنة بدلاً من الأحكام المطلقة. من أمثلتها: One could argue that، It is often claimed that، is likely to، tends to، to a certain extent. يميل بعض المتحدثين بالعربية إلى التعميم بعبارات مثل All people أو Always، بينما يفضّل الممتحنون صيغاً أكثر دقة مثل Many people tend to.
examples: It is often claimed that social media makes young people less sociable.
Remote learning is likely to become more common over the next decade.
To a certain extent, the government is responsible for reducing inequality.

words.ex: According to the band descriptors, you need a wide range of idiomatic language for Band 8.
There was some hesitation in Part 3, but it was mostly natural.
You self-corrected quickly when you used the wrong tense.
Varying your intonation makes you sound more engaged.
Your lexical resource was strong, especially with collocations.
Let's set a target for your next mock exam: fewer filler words.

dialogue.t: Well done for completing the full mock exam. How do you feel it went overall?
Better than I expected. I felt more confident when I was describing the photos than when I had to answer the abstract questions at the end.
That matches my notes. Your fluency was good, but there was some hesitation in Part 4. What happened in the long turn?
If I'd had more time, I would have added a clearer conclusion. I ran out of ideas after about ninety seconds.
Your lexical resource was impressive, and you self-corrected well. Your intonation was a little flat at times, though.
I think the area I need to work on most is pronunciation, especially stressing key words.
Agreed. So what target would you like to set?
Next time I'll focus on varying my intonation and using a few linking phrases to buy myself thinking time instead of pausing.

grammar.title: Third and mixed conditionals for reflection
grammar.ar: نستخدم الشرط الثالث (If + had + التصريف الثالث، would have + التصريف الثالث) للتحدث عن ماضٍ لم يحدث وتخيّل نتيجته المختلفة، وهو مثالي لتقييم أدائك بعد الامتحان. أما الشرط المختلط فيربط شرطاً في الماضي بنتيجة في الحاضر، مثل: If I had practised more, I would be more confident now. يخطئ كثيرون فيضعون would في جملة if، والصحيح أن تبقى would في جملة النتيجة فقط.
examples: If I had prepared more examples, I would have spoken for the full two minutes.
If I'd listened to the question carefully, I wouldn't have misunderstood it.
If I had started practising earlier, I would feel much calmer now.

words.ex: A well-chosen anecdote can captivate an audience within the first thirty seconds.
The discovery of penicillin was a groundbreaking moment in the history of medicine.
Many inventions, from the microwave to Post-it notes, owe their existence to serendipity.
It may sound counterintuitive, but some bacteria are essential for our health.
Al-Khwarizmi played a pivotal role in the development of algebra.
Before going into detail, I'll briefly outline the three main parts of my talk.

dialogue.t: Right, imagine I'm your audience and I've just sat down. How would you open your talk on the invention of the camera?
Have you ever stopped to consider that the basic principle behind your phone camera was described over a thousand years ago?
Oh, that's intriguing. By whom?
Believe it or not, it was Ibn al-Haytham, a scientist in eleventh-century Cairo, who explained how light passes through a tiny hole to form an image.
That's a strong hook. Now, how will you let us know where the talk is going?
What I'd like to do today is trace the journey from his camera obscura to the modern smartphone.
I'll begin by explaining his experiments, before moving on to the first photographs in the nineteenth century, and finally I'll look at how digital sensors changed everything.
Excellent — a striking fact, a clear purpose and a roadmap. That's exactly what a good opening needs.

grammar.title: Cleft sentences with 'What' for emphasis
grammar.ar: الجملة المشقوقة (Cleft sentence) تبدأ بـ What وتُستخدم لتسليط الضوء على المعلومة الأهم في نهاية الجملة. التركيب هو: What + فاعل + فعل + is/was + المعلومة المهمة. فبدلاً من قول I'd like to explain... نقول What I'd like to do is explain... فيبدو الكلام أكثر رسمية وتشويقاً. لاحظ أن الفعل بعد is يأتي غالباً في صيغة المصدر بدون to.
examples: What I'd like to do today is explore how a single accident led to a medical revolution.
What surprised scientists most was how quickly the vaccine took effect.
What makes this invention so remarkable is its simplicity.

words.ex: Urban sprawl has pushed residential areas further and further into the desert.
The oil boom triggered a massive influx of workers from across the world.
Building infrastructure such as metros and highways became an urgent priority.
Rapid population growth has put a strain on water and electricity supplies.
Dependence on private cars has exacerbated traffic congestion in many Gulf cities.
Planners are now looking for more sustainable ways to manage growth.

dialogue.t: You've just finished explaining the oil boom. How do you move on to the next section?
Turning now to the second major cause, I'd like to look at the huge influx of foreign workers from the 1970s onwards.
Good. And how does that connect to the effects?
As a direct consequence, cities like Dubai and Doha expanded at an extraordinary rate, which put enormous strain on housing and transport.
To put this into perspective, Dubai's population grew from around 60,000 in 1960 to well over three million today.
That's a powerful figure. What comes after that?
This brings me to my next point, namely the environmental impact. Building on what I said earlier about car dependence, urban sprawl has significantly increased carbon emissions.
Very clear. Your listener always knows exactly where they are in the talk.

grammar.title: Participle clauses for cause and result
grammar.ar: تُستخدم جمل اسم الفاعل (Participle clauses) لربط السبب بالنتيجة بأسلوب أكاديمي مختصر. نستخدم صيغة -ing لحدث متزامن أو نتيجة، وHaving + التصريف الثالث لحدث وقع قبل غيره. يجب أن يكون فاعل الجملتين واحداً، فلا نقول: Having grown rapidly, the traffic increased إذا كانت المدينة هي التي نمت. هذا الأسلوب يجعل العرض أكثر سلاسة من تكرار because وso.
examples: Having expanded so rapidly, the city struggled to provide adequate public transport.
Attracted by high salaries, millions of workers moved to the region.
The population doubled within a decade, putting immense pressure on public services.

words.ex: The cost of solar panels plummeted between 2010 and 2020.
Youth unemployment rose steadily before levelling off in 2019.
There was a dramatic surge in wind energy investment after 2015.
Oil prices fluctuated considerably throughout the period shown.
A growing proportion of the national budget is now allocated to renewables.
Solar power accounted for nearly half of all new investment in 2022.

dialogue.t: Here's the chart on renewable energy investment in the Middle East. What do you notice first?
By far the most striking feature is the dramatic growth in solar investment over the last decade.
Can you be more specific about the figures?
Certainly. Investment rose sharply between 2015 and 2019, from roughly two billion to almost nine billion dollars.
It then levelled off during 2020, probably due to the pandemic, before surging again in 2021.
And what about fossil fuel investment on the same chart?
As the figures clearly illustrate, it plummeted between 2014 and 2016. This would appear to indicate that the region is gradually shifting its long-term priorities.
Nice use of cautious language there — you're interpreting the data without overclaiming.

grammar.title: Hedging: presenting conclusions cautiously
grammar.ar: في العروض الأكاديمية لا نقدّم الاستنتاجات كحقائق مطلقة، بل نستخدم أسلوب التحوّط (Hedging) لإظهار الدقة والموضوعية. من أهم أدواته: would appear to / seem to، والأفعال الناقصة مثل may وmight وcould، والظروف مثل arguably وapparently. هذا يختلف عن الأسلوب المباشر الشائع في العربية، لكنه يُعدّ علامة على المستوى المتقدم في الإنجليزية.
examples: This would appear to indicate that government incentives are having a positive effect.
The decline may well be linked to changes in education policy.
It could be argued that the figures underestimate the true level of youth unemployment.

words.ex: In layman's terms, inflation means your money buys less than it used to.
Comparing the heart to a pump is a simple but effective analogy.

words.ar: يتلخّص في / يرجع في جوهره إلى
words.ex: The whole debate boils down to one question: who pays the cost?
Melting ice creates a feedback loop that speeds up global warming.
When prices rise faster than wages, people's purchasing power falls.
The app uses an algorithm to recommend videos based on what you've watched.

dialogue.t: Let's say I know nothing about technology. Could you explain machine learning to me?
Of course. In layman's terms, it's a way of teaching computers to learn from examples rather than following fixed instructions.
Hmm, I'm still not quite sure what that looks like in practice.
The easiest way to picture this is to think about how a child learns to recognise cats. Nobody gives them a list of rules — they just see lots of cats.
Think of it as the computer looking at thousands of photos labelled 'cat' or 'not cat' until it starts spotting the patterns by itself.
Ah, so it improves through experience?
Exactly. Essentially, a machine learning system works by adjusting itself every time it makes a mistake. In other words, what this boils down to is practice, just like us.
That analogy made it really clear. I could actually explain that to someone else now.

grammar.title: Imagine / Suppose + conditionals for explaining
grammar.ar: عند شرح فكرة معقدة نطلب من المستمع أن يتخيّل موقفاً مألوفاً باستخدام Imagine (that) أو Suppose أو Picture. بعدها نستخدم الشرط الصفري (If + مضارع، مضارع) للحقائق العامة، أو الشرط الثاني (If + ماضٍ، would) للمواقف الافتراضية. هذا الأسلوب يربط المفهوم المجرد بتجربة يعرفها الجمهور فيسهل فهمه.
examples: Imagine that every time you put a coin in a jar, it shrinks a little — that's essentially what inflation does to savings.
Suppose you heated a room and the heat made the heater work even harder; that's how a feedback loop operates.
If you show the program enough examples, it gradually learns to make accurate predictions.

words.ex: She raised a valid concern about the cost of the project.
A detailed analysis of the economics is beyond the scope of this presentation.
Could you elaborate on how the system would be funded?
I'll concede that the initial costs are high, but the savings are significant.
I can only offer a tentative answer until more research is available.
Sorry, could you rephrase the question? I want to make sure I understand.

dialogue.t: Thank you for your talk on desalination. But isn't it true that the leftover salt water harms marine life?
That's a very valid point — let me address it by explaining how newer plants dilute the brine before releasing it.
Fine, but are these plants actually affordable for poorer countries?
If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether the technology can be used outside wealthy Gulf states?
Yes, exactly. And would solar-powered plants work on a large scale?
I'd need to look into that further, but my sense is that costs are falling fast enough to make it realistic within the next decade.
One last thing — how does this affect global water politics?
That's beyond the scope of my talk, although I would say that greater water independence could certainly reduce tensions between some countries.

grammar.title: Indirect questions: word order
grammar.ar: عند إعادة صياغة سؤال أو التحقق منه نستخدم السؤال غير المباشر، وفيه يأتي الفاعل قبل الفعل كما في الجملة الخبرية، أي لا يوجد قلب ولا do/does/did. نستخدم whether أو if للأسئلة التي جوابها نعم/لا، وأدوات الاستفهام مثل how وwhy لغيرها. خطأ شائع لدى المتحدثين بالعربية: you're asking how much does it cost، والصحيح: you're asking how much it costs.
examples: If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether the project can be completed on time.
I'm not entirely sure why the costs increased so dramatically.
Could you tell me what evidence you're basing that claim on?

words.ex: The rationale behind the scheme is to reduce traffic in the city centre.
With current technology, the plan is entirely feasible.
The long-term benefits clearly outweigh the initial investment.
We consulted all the key stakeholders, including residents and local businesses.
The council will launch a pilot scheme in two neighbourhoods first.
The idea is scalable, so it could be applied to other cities later.

dialogue.t: So, tell us about the project you're proposing for Riyadh.
I'm proposing a network of shaded, solar-powered bus stops with cooling systems and live travel information.
The rationale behind this proposal is simple: people avoid public transport in summer because waiting outside in 45-degree heat is unbearable.
But plenty of cities have bus shelters. Why is yours different?
What sets this apart is that each stop generates its own electricity, so the cooling costs the city almost nothing to run.
Surely the installation costs would be enormous, though?
They're significant, but the potential benefits far outweigh the initial expense — fewer cars, cleaner air and a healthier population. We'd start with a pilot scheme on two main routes.
To sum up, this project is not only feasible but also essential if we want people to choose public transport.

grammar.title: Not only ... but also (with inversion)
grammar.ar: يُستخدم التركيب not only ... but also لإضافة فكرة ثانية أقوى من الأولى. وعندما نبدأ الجملة بـ Not only للتأكيد في الأسلوب الرسمي يجب قلب الفاعل والفعل كما في السؤال، أي نضع الفعل المساعد (is / does / will...) قبل الفاعل. أما إذا جاء not only في وسط الجملة فلا يحدث قلب. هذا الأسلوب يمنح خاتمة العرض قوة وإقناعاً.
examples: To sum up, the plan is not only feasible but also highly cost-effective.
Not only would the project reduce emissions, but it would also create hundreds of local jobs.
Not only does the design save energy, but it also improves the quality of life for residents.

units.cando: Can develop a complex argument systematically, highlighting significant points with relevant supporting detail, and can counter opposing views persuasively while conceding points diplomatically.
lessons: Building a Watertight Case
Learner argues whether secondary schools should replace some exams with long-term research projects, structuring claims, reasons and evidence.
The crux of my argument is that ...; This is borne out by the fact that ...; It follows, therefore, that ...; Not only does ..., but it also ...
Conceding Without Losing Ground
Learner debates whether social media influencers are positive role models, acknowledging valid counterpoints before reasserting a position.
Granted, ... ; that said, ...; While there is some truth in the idea that ..., it overlooks ...; I'd go along with that up to a point, but ...; Admittedly ..., yet ...
Rebuttal and Challenging Assumptions
In a mock debate on banning smartphones in classrooms, the learner identifies flaws in the tutor's reasoning and responds tactfully.
That argument rests on the assumption that ...; I'm not sure that necessarily follows, because ...; If we take that to its logical conclusion, ...; With respect, the evidence suggests otherwise: ...
Hedging and Degrees of Certainty
Learner discusses predictions about remote learning and AI tutors, calibrating confidence precisely rather than speaking in absolutes.
It would seem that ...; There's every likelihood that ...; It's by no means certain that ...; ... is bound to ..., although ... may well ...; To all intents and purposes, ...
Weighing Ethical Dilemmas
Learner explores whether genetic screening, wealth inequality or animal testing can be justified, balancing principles and consequences.
On the one hand, ... could be justified on the grounds that ...; Where do we draw the line between ... and ...?; The moral dimension here is ...; Were we to ..., the consequences might be ...
Full Formal Debate
Learner takes a side on 'This house believes that university should be free for everyone', delivering an opening, rebuttal and closing statement.
I stand firmly in favour of / opposed to the motion because ...; My opponent has claimed that ..., but ...; Let me draw your attention to ...; In light of everything we've heard, ...

units.t: Academic Presentations and Explaining Complex Ideas
units.cando: Can give clear, well-structured presentations on complex subjects, expanding and supporting points of view with subsidiary points, reasons and examples, and handle follow-up questions spontaneously.
lessons: Hooking Your Audience
Learner opens a short talk on a scientific discovery or invention using a striking fact, question or anecdote, then outlines the structure.
Have you ever stopped to consider ...?; Believe it or not, ...; What I'd like to do today is ...; I'll begin by ..., before moving on to ..., and finally ...
Signposting and Logical Flow
Learner presents the causes and effects of rapid urbanisation in Gulf cities, guiding the listener clearly between sections.
Turning now to ...; This brings me to my next point, namely ...; Building on what I said earlier, ...; As a direct consequence, ...; To put this into perspective, ...
Describing Data and Trends
Learner interprets a chart about renewable energy investment or youth employment, highlighting key figures and drawing conclusions.
As the figures clearly illustrate, ...; ... rose sharply / levelled off / plummeted between ... and ...; By far the most striking feature is ...; This would appear to indicate that ...
Simplifying the Complex
Learner explains an abstract concept (e.g. inflation, machine learning, climate feedback loops) to a non-specialist audience using analogies.
In layman's terms, ...; Think of it as ...; The easiest way to picture this is ...; In other words, what this boils down to is ...; Essentially, ... works by ...
Handling Q&A with Confidence
After a mini-presentation, the tutor asks challenging or unexpected questions; the learner buys time, clarifies and answers convincingly.

That's a very valid point — let me address it by ...; If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether ...; I'd need to look into that further, but my sense is that ...; That's beyond the scope of my talk, although ...
Delivering a Polished Talk
Learner gives a 4-5 minute presentation on an innovation project they would propose for their city, followed by questions and feedback.
The rationale behind this proposal is ...; What sets this apart is ...; The potential benefits far outweigh ...; To sum up, ... is not only feasible but also ...

units.t: Global Issues, Society and the Future
units.cando: Can express themselves fluently and spontaneously on abstract and complex topics, using language flexibly and effectively to speculate, evaluate and relate ideas to broader social contexts.
lessons: Tradition Meets Transformation
